speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
that Bill C-23, an act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to a Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, again this is a rather straightforward bill. It is a technical bill. I do not intend to speak long on the bill, just perhaps a few introductory remarks and then some specifics on the bill.
As most people in the country will know, the Canadian Wheat Board is a Crown corporation that is over 50 years old. It is a well-run Crown corporation. It operates very independently of government and operates with a head office in Winnipeg with five commissioners that are appointed by the federal government but once ap-
Govemment Orders
pointed, operate very independently from government.
Over the years the commissioners have been responsible for the marketing of, first of all, wheat, then barley, then oats and latterly, just wheat and barley. They are the sole marketer of wheat and barley now in the international market, so that anything a barley or wheat producer in the designated area, which is basically western Canada, produces and wants to sell for export has to go through the Canadian Wheat Board.
Additionally, producers in the Wheat Board designated area that wish to sell for domestic human consumption also have to go through the Canadian Wheat Board. So the Canadian Wheat Board plays a very large role in the life of rural western Canada. It has over the years established a very good reputation as a selling agency. It regularly sells to some 60 countries around the world and, as I said, has developed a reputation second to none for being able to execute any contract or agreement it signs with a country or a customer. Their reputation as far as delivering on that agreement is very good. That has served us well over the years in terms of maintaining our market share even though prices have been very depressed.
There were concerns raised in 1989 and 1990 by the Auditor General as to the type of authority that the Canadian Wheat Board had from the Parliament of Canada for credit. As things have changed internationally, the use of the credit has become much more of a factor in international sales. Many countries offer concessional credit. By that I mean credit that is below prevailing rates of interest for long time periods at rates below commercial credit. The Wheat Board is not in the business of operating with concessional credit, but it has been able to make use of credit to increase its sales. As economic conditions have changed in the world, the use of credit has become much more of a factor.
There was a time when less than 10 per cent of the board's operations was based on credit. We are in a situation now where closer to 20 or 25 per cent of the board's operations is based on credit.
Bill C-23 simply provides for proper parliamentary authority with respect to its accounts receivable arising from credit grain sales that are approved by cabinet. This simply means that the Canadian Wheat Board as a Crown agency operates with guarantees from the Government of Canada. It has been doing this since 1972

October 8, 1991
Government Orders
when the minister of the day sent a letter of comfort to the board, in effect saying to the board that because we, the Government of Canada, have agreed with you, you can continue to sell on credit. We regularly established lines of credit for various countries around the world based on all kinds of things, but mostly the number of tonnes or the number of bushels a country is going to provide for us and our estimate of the need for credit.
Therefore, when we provided this credit the Auditor General was concerned that we did not have the proper parliamentary authority for the government and the Parliament of Canada to grant the credit to the Canadian Wheat Board that it needed to operate properly. Therefore, we are proposing to amend section 19 of the Wheat Board Act to provide proper parliamentary authority for the Wheat Board to use the credit it needs more and more to be able to sell.
Basically, it is a technical amendment. It means that the board will continue to operate in exactly the same way that it has in the past, except that we are responding to concerns raised by the Auditor General to put what he considers a better legal basis for that type of operation to continue.
The second amendment is under section 33 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I should explain that one of the main principles under which the Canadian Wheat Board operates is the use of a pooling or an averaging system. So, whether a producer sells at the beginning of a crop year, which is August 1, or he sells at the end, which is July 31, a 12-month period, a producer will receive the same price per bushel and the same price per tonne that he would have if he had sold at any other time during the year.
They do this on the basis of a pooling or an averaging system. When a producer takes a load of grain into an elevator and sells, for instance, on September 15 or October 8, he receives what is called an initial payment for that product. Throughout the crop year the Canadian Wheat Board then goes ahead and sells and takes all the prices it receives for the various products it sells to different countries, and you can understand that the price will vary over a 12-month period. At the end of the 12-month period, it does the arithmetic to arrive at an average price. As long as the average price for the product the producer has sold throughout the 12-month period is more than the initial payment, the producer receives a final payment. The final payments are usually
available three or four months after the closing of the crop year.
Again the Auditor General was concerned that the Canadian Wheat Board did not have the proper legal basis, the proper parliamentary approval to go ahead and make final payments until, as the Auditor General said, payment had been received in full. Under this amendment to section 33, we are providing a legal basis for that to occur. I think everybody would agree that if you are going to provide a loan and it is guaranteed by the Government of Canada that once those moneys are advanced or borrowed by the Canadian Wheat Board, they should then be in a position to go ahead and make final payments even though the repayment of the moneys owing on sales that had been made in a previous crop year have not yet been received.
Just to summarize, we are providing better parliamentary authority for the Canadian Wheat Board to operate in two areas; first, as a result of a guarantee by the Government of Canada, the granting of credit to various countries and customers that the Canadian Wheat Board sells to; second, once that credit is granted, to provide whatis considered a better parliamentary authority for the Canadian Wheat Board to distribute funds to producers once the sale has been concluded.
This does not alter the way the Canadian Wheat Board operates with regard to any of its procedures, whether it is the pooling system or the way they sell or the way they deal with customers. It is simply responding to two concerns that the Auditor General raised in both 1989 and 1990 with regard to two sections of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, namely section 19 and section 33. That is what Bill C-23 does today.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to say a few words on Bill C-23.
The minister suggested that this is just a technical amendment. I guess anything that we do in this House is a technical amendment from the point of view that it is changing a clause or a word or a sentence in a bill, but clearly this matter that is before the House today was important enough that the Auditor General raised it both in his 1989 and 1990 reports. He pointed out that the Government of Canada had not sought parliamentary authority to guarantee $4.2 billion owing to the Canadian Wheat Board. If this is only a technical amendment, it is the largest technical amendment in
October 8, 1991

history when we look at the $4.2 billion owing to the Canadian Wheat Board and not having parliamentary authority.
It is a very important issue and certainly one that the Auditor General has picked up on two occasions. Clearly the necessity of passing this legislation is apparent.
I think most of us in this country are very supportive of the Canadian Wheat Board because it provides a great deal of stability in the way we market our grains in this country, especially in western Canada. There are similar wheat boards, not quite the same but of a similar nature, in Ontario and in some of the other provinces, but the granddaddy of them all, of course, is the Canadian Wheat Board which operates in the four western provinces and brings a great deal of stability to that industry.
Without the Canadian Wheat Board, I think our ability to compete in international grain markets would be sharply diminished. We not only have the expertise of this agency, which is able to move into all kinds of markets that individual producers would not have the opportunity to do, but it provides stability to the marketplace. Without it we would have four or five big grain companies carving up the market and seeing how they could drive down the price.
In this way the Canadian Wheat Board offers producers right across the prairies a stability which they, in my opinion, could never achieve. We only have to look at some of the grains and oilseeds which are not under the Wheat Board authority to see how they are able to carve up the markets to their advantage.
I think that whatever we can do to strengthen and support the Canadian Wheat Board is very important. Even though it is really a farmers' agency for the marketing of their grains, it is under the authority of the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds. I was pleased this morning to see him supporting the Canadian Wheat Board because he has not always been seen as a great supporter of it. Clearly when he took oats away from the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board he was seen as very unsupportive of the board, and I don't think farmers have benefited by the removal of oats from the board. It was seen as something to give away to those who are
Government Orders
opposed to the Canadian Wheat Board after the 1988 general election.
The various grain producing associations or groups in the west who were opposed to it pressed the minister to give them something in return for the support that they gave him in the free trade debate and the general election of 1988. And so oats was removed from the authority of the Board, even though the Canadian Wheat Board Act itself really provides for wheat but barley has historically been under the authority of the board as has been oats.
This is a very important piece of legislation from the point of view that it gives legal authority to the Wheat Board to make sales internationally. We have never faced such a disaster in grain prices in history. Those of us who work in the field of agriculture in the House of Commons complain that regardless of how serious the disaster is, that seldom if ever is it carried on the national news. Certainly it is never carried to any extent in the major daily papers like The Toronto Star. However, the disaster in Canadian grain and oilseeds has been so intense this fall that we have seen a three-day period of full page coverage in The Toronto Star and major stories in other newspapers as well as major coverage on the national news. I guess we are glad to see this coverage from the point of view of agriculture being reported in the daily and national press. We are sorry to see it covered because of the magnitude of the calamity, the disaster facing this industry today.
I spoke earlier about the need for orderly marketing. That is what every agriculture group, certainly the producer groups, are seeking in the international realm today and that is what we hope will ultimately come out of the negotiations at the multilateral trade negotiations in Geneva this fall. If it does not, the disaster which is facing our producers will continue.
We have seen a quantum decline in the production of grain and the viability of the industry in countries like Argentina and Australia, and to some extent Canada faces the same kind of financial disaster because our exports are so large-some 80 per cent of our production goes into export sales-relative to the size of our urban society, and ultimately the resources of the country come from all sectors of society. Clearly the European Community with its 340 million people, the United States with its 250 million people, have more capacity per capita

Government Orders
to withstand the kind of international trading war that we have faced since 1985. The United States decided in their farm bill in 1985 that it was going to bludgeon the European Economic Community into submission and stop the export subsidies.
Unfortunately it has not succeeded. It has spent billions of dollars. This year the commitment is $900 million. Next year it will be $1.2 billion. God only knows how much the European Community has spent. In any event, that trade war goes on and on and on.
For farmers in Canada this year the initial price is the lowest in 16 years at $95 a tonne for No. 1 red spring wheat. It is less than half of what it was 10 years ago. Of course the cost of production has probably doubled in those 10 years, leaving farmers in the most desperate situation which we have seen in a lifetime.
That is why we see parades of tractors 30 miles long south of Lethbridge in Alberta on our televisions screens. That is why we saw mass rallies of farmers, 3,000 or 4,000 strong, last week at Rosetown, Saskatchewan, to protest the lack of action by the Government of Canada.
We do not know when the government is going to act. Clearly it must act soon. We thought the kind of proposal the government made last spring before the House of Commons would be carried through, that the government would provide a third line of defence. There were three mechanisms inculcated in the safety net system. One was the Gross Revenue Insurance Program which was to provide a guarantee to producers of gross revenue per acre, so that regardless of whether the world price for wheat went down or whether there was a drought and production was low, there would be a sort of gross revenue income mechanism.
Then there was a second provision, the NISA, the Net Income Stabilization Account. It was to allow farmers to put money into a stabilization account which was to be matched by the two senior levels of government to ensure stability over a long period of time based on some
2 per cent of their gross sales and allowing for additional contributions.
For 1991 the third element was the most important. That was the third line of defence, a mechanism to provide an injection of cash when the first two systems failed to function.
If there ever was an occasion when the third line of defence mechanism should have triggered, it was last spring. Producer group after producer group came before the agriculture committee that studied this bill and said: "We agree generally with the GRIP and NISA proposals, the first two lines of defence, but there is a problem. They are for the 1991-92 crop year. Our problem is the 1990-91 crop year, the crop that was grown last year".
Unfortunately 1990 was the year the United States export enhancement program provided the maximum amount of subsidy and drove world prices down well below $100 a tonne.
The exact figures are not known yet, but it is way below the cost of any reasonable production.
At the same that those world prices for grain and oilseed commodities were going through the floor boards, the government was reducing its support program in western Canada by $1 billion.
At the same time in eastern Canada they were reducing their support program by $300 million. Every grain and oilseed group that came before the agriculture committee said: "Look, we agree with those two first lines of defence for stabilization of our grain and oilseed economy. The problem is that the 1990 crop year has been such a disaster. There has been such a pulverizing of farm income that there must be a third line of defence".
This spring we want to see an immediate cash injection of assistance not only to cover the reduction in price of the grain, but to cover the reduction in support programs which the federal government unloaded on Canadian producers.
The government brought in a program called FSAM, Farmer Stabilization and Assistance Measures. Unfortunately, there is a very small amount of cash in that system and none of it has been delivered. It is a

Government Orders
mechanism to reduce premiums. Big deal. There never were any premiums on programs like the special grains measure. There never were any premiums on programs like drought assistance in 1989.
Those programs provided for crop cover programs but the actual cash is a very small portion. It is a kind of mixed up measure under the Net Income Stabilization Account program. The assistant deputy minister told us in the agriculture committee back in late August that they hope to have some cheques out by Christmas.
Christmas is far too late. We want the assistance now, we want it in cash and it must come.
We are really facing a very difficult time in the whole grain and oilseeds industry. The government has removed oats from the Canadian Wheat Board and the United States is bludgeoning us daily with the Export Enhancement Program. The Minister of Agriculture is quoted as saying he is going to take retaliatory action against the European Community by the end of this year if the subsidy war continues.
It is strange to me that no action has been taken against the United States. Although the Europeans are a major grain producer now, they were not in the 1950s. I still believe that the United States has a more profound influence on what the world price of grain will be.
I would hope that since the government has entered into a free trade agreement that it will take the same retaliatory action against the United States as it is taking against the EEC.
Clearly the biggest player on the block is the United States. The European Community is important but the same action should be taken against both governments.
The Canadian Wheat Board is playing an important part in distributing income fairly among the producers so that whenever a producer markets his grain, whether it is in the fall or the spring, if it is of similar quality and category it will receive the same benefit.
This legislation which is before us today will legitimize the credits which the federal government has provided in the past for those sales abroad which amount to billions and billions of dollars. We hope that the price of grain will soon rise so it will be even more billions of dollars and those producers will have an adequate return for their investment, their labour and their expertise.
The second part of course is that it provides for the funds to be paid off and the credit to be provided before the pool account can be closed and those payments of both principal and interest are made.
We support the bill. It is of a technical nature. It is one that is very important because obviously we seek markets around the world in eastern Europe, Poland and other areas, especially the Soviet republics. This legal authority for sales of grain will be important in the years ahead. It will provide an adequate and proper legal authority from Parliament to give credit to the Canadian Wheat Board for the excellent job it does of marketing our grain abroad.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the amendment that is being proposed to the Canadian Wheat Board today which has the effect of correcting an anomaly that has existed. It puts into words and into law by authority of this House of Commons the authority of the Canadian Wheat board to make sales on credit, the contingent liability of which rests with the Government of Canada. In fact it does not change anything in terms of the operations of the Wheat Board. Since 1972 when the then minister Otto Lang sent a letter to the board authorizing them to make credit sales, it has done so. It has not shown those credit sales in any way as a liability to producer accounts. It has always assumed that the payments were made on time even when they were not because the Government of Canada, in the eyes of the Wheat Board and in the eyes of the farmers, had already committed itself to being liable for any shortfall or any inability of a borrowing country to make payments on time.
From the point of view of the Wheat Board the payments to the producers were made annually as if the sale had been completed and as if the account for the loan was up to date.
Not only did they consider that the loans were up to date but they also had to consider, for purposes of accounting, the surpluses that would accrue annually to the farmers which are paid out as a final payment.
They considered that interest due on the loans was also up to date and received and the Government of Canada made certain that the cash flow persisted and existed to make the Wheat Board accounts good so that

Government Orders
those final payment cheques would in fact be good cheques.
The only thing wrong with this process that has been going on almost 20 years according to the Auditor General is that the authority of the House is never asked for. Today with the amendments the government is putting before the House it is asking for the approval of the House for the Governor in Council, that is the cabinet, to in fact provide the loan guarantees that have been a fact of life in the conduct of international grain trade since 1972.
There are some questions of course that this raises. In 1972 there were no qualms anywhere about extending credit to purchasing countries. The world economy seemed to be going into an upward spin which is now sometimes described by some economists as an inflation-aiy cycle. At any rate, in 1972 going into debt was not considered a problem by any of the borrowing countries which needed the food in any case and had very little choice except to feed their people.
That contingent liability has accumulated to the point where in the last Auditor General's report he pointed out that the government still had not received parliamentary approval for a guarantee of $4.2 billion which is owed to the Canadian Wheat Board to finance troubled foreign countries.
I was told by officials out in the hall today that that contingent liability accumulation is now in the neighbourhood of $4.6 billion. That is not necessarily in the form of bad accounts, it is simply in the form of loans that have been extended, and some of them are being kept up to date and some of them are not.
It raises some problem for all of us as parliamentarians because it is this body here that authorizes the expenditures of money and when we have a contingent liability, as we have in this case, Parliament does not, in my view, seem to have a very good way of handling this kind of authorization. All we can do on an annual basis is see a number in the budget which might be applied for possible bad loans or possible default and approve that on an annual basis.
We have no way that I am aware of that easily tells us as parliamentarians how much contingent liability we are backing as a country at the end of any one year. With a great deal of diligent research one might find it going
through all of the agencies and departments and various commitments to foreign debt and foreign loans that the Government of Canada has made, but we really do not have an accumulative total that tells us as parliamentarians just where we are going.
I know that in good times none of us as private citizens or as people acting as representatives of private citizens really spent too much time worrying about the notes that we have co-signed or the contingent liabilities that we have taken on. But as the debt situation in the world and the apparent recession fills more and more countries, it is something that we would probably have to be aware of. That is one of the things that this particular legislation brings to mind in that we know and we realize in this House that it is absolutely vital that the Government of Canada stand behind the export trade credits that organizations like the Canadian Wheat Board incur. There are a number of other loans that we make through other agencies and through other departments which are vital to the continuance of the Canadian economy and to the ability of importing countries to buy our products. It has both commercial justification and human rights justification.
A lot of the countries that buy Canadian food, for instance, have to do it on the basis of long-term credit. They are not paying for the food when it is consumed. They are committing themselves to a long-term debt to pay for the food that has been consumed in the year that it was imported. There is really no choice for those countries except to import food other than to watch their population starve.
As I say, it has basic human rights. Questions have to be answered with this question of contingent liability and loans. We also as parliamentarians are responsible for the money that taxpayers expend and those taxpayers expect us as their representatives to have a handle on how much of these commitments we have been making and to have a handle on how we expect to handle the situation if foreign governments and foreign customers are unable to make the payments. The whole system of these loans and the trade that is incurred by credit sales makes some assumptions about the viability of the international monetary system, the kinds of guarantees that each country provides to each other to make sure that their currency is still sound and that their credit is still good.
October 8, 1991

As I said earlier in my remarks, this whole system is becoming a little more fragile as the recession sinks in, as countries whose economies appear to be going through a vast disruption, countries such as those in central and eastern Europe, but also countries in Africa that have been going through drought, famine and civil war and the apparent collapse of their social, economic and political structure. When all is said and done, these countries do need our food.
It is in the best interests of the country for this Parliament to grant the authority that we all thought was in place over the last 19 years to back the loans and guarantee the loans that the Canadian Wheat Board makes to finalize sales to countries which need food and our products but do not have the immediate cash, and that this continue.
The farmers of this country recognize that this is of assistance to their efforts to produce food for hungry people and to facilitate the movement of that food from their farms to the mouths of those hungry people. I believe it will generally be applauded. As I have said, as parliamentarians we also have to find a better way of handling the whole question of contingent liability because we do have concerns and responsibilities to our taxpayers for not only the accumulated debt of the country which seems to be fairly clear cut-we can count that, it is now over $400 billion-but we have no immediate way, without a great deal of research, to find the accumulated contingent liabilities of all the departments and all the commitments we have made through agencies on behalf of ourselves as the Government of Canada.
I simply wanted to point that out as a question that has to be answered for backbenchers and ministers as well if this Parliament is going to continue with its function of approving all of the expenditures and all the commitments the executive branch makes on our behalf.
I applaud the government for bringing this legislation to the House and requesting approval to grant cabinet the authority to make these loans, which it has been making over the last 19 years.
I am pleased that with the passage of this legislation we will have followed the proper procedure of going to Parliament before the expenditure of money takes place.
Government Orders

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the two points the hon. member was making at the end, if he wants to look at page 48 of the last annual report of the Canadian Wheat Board, he will see that there is a number shown there about one third of the way down the page that shows $4,625 billion. It says: "See note 2." That in effect is a listing of the contingent liability of the Canadian Wheat Board.
In the case of this Crown corporation it does not take a lot of work to dig this out because it regularly publishes it. He will also note that the year previous it was $3.7 billion. So, it is shown very clearly as a continent liability. Nobody is trying to disguise anything. It is there for full public disclosure.
Second just to make the point, and I will just speak for the board, when the Canadian Wheat Board makes a grain sale to a country and the country signs the guarantee, it is considered sovereign debt and ultimately collectable or repayable. That is the position that we take as a government and that is consistent, as I understand it, with accounting procedures. Now, there have been cases in the past where there has been rescheduling through an agreement, the Paris Club is an example, where some of this debt has been set aside. That is by general agreement of all the countries involved and one has to deal with whatever is going to be rescheduled or set aside at that time.
Just to make two points: The contingent liability for the Canadian Wheat Board is shown and published in every annual report. The loans that the board makes are to other sovereign countries and are therefore ultimately repayable. So if anything changes, then that has to be reflected in the way the Government of Canada keeps its books.

I do not think anything I said contravened the information that the minister re-entered on the table. The point that I had been very much aware of, and in fact I used some of the figures from the Wheat Board's annual report, was that it provides accurate figures on the contingent liability of the Government of Canada, as do most of the other agencies. It is just that when we come to passing budgets in this House, private members of Parliament are generally not confronted through the budget documents with the accumulated contingent liabilities from all of the various agencies and

Government Orders
departments that have accrued over the intervening years. We do have a final figure for the national debt, we do have final figures for a whole host of things, but we generally don't get a list of the accumulated contingent liabilities from all of the various nations with which we deal. I reiterate from my speech, this has generally not been of any concern to anyone because all of the countries of the world had, until very recently, been considered not to be having any great difficulty as sovereign nations meeting their debts and obligations.
That is changing, however, with the onset of this last recession or depression and will probably require some consideration from this House, and from the Ministry of Finance, as to how to present those contingent liabilities for the approval of this Chamber in the coming years. The situation is changing and not all of those loans and liabilities are going to be repaid on time. We are still presuming that all of those sovereign nations will still exist and that the debt will be recognized and honoured, but that changes over time as well.
We may in fact find ourselves having to write off some of them, although I think that the debts which have accrued through the sale of Wheat Board grains, wheat, oats and barley until recently-now it is just wheat and barley-have been made with due appreciation of the ability of the debtor to repay the debt.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, Eglinton-Lawrence is not in the farming community but I felt I had to intervene in this debate. I have been impressed by the fact that the debate has been so gentlemanly, with all due deference to the female members in this House, that there has been a tone of courtesy and deference from one side to the other, and you know, Mr. Speaker, I really cannot understand it.
We are talking about a bill that has enormous consequence for one of the major resource industries of this country, for one of the major social components of the fabric of this nation, a fabric that is being tom apart by international affairs, international conditions, and by our own domestic problems. And everybody is very polite. The minister says we are only dealing with a technical change. The tone is muted. Attention is vivid. We have members on both sides talking about relativity of some problems from one sector to another, as if this were an academic exercise.
About the only thing that I heard that was of significance is what my hon. colleague who just finished speaking said about members of Parliament in this House being responsible for expenditures from this Parliament and this government.
He is right because we are responsible for every cent that we spend. There is not one cent that is better spent than those that we spend on our own citizens, whether we do it through ensuring credit sales or whether we do it in outright relief.
At this moment in Canada in the agricultural community, farmers require assistance by this government. We have the highest quality of wheat and grains in the world. Bar none, bar none. We are very efficient in the way that we produce those products and yet we have no sales.
We have an anomaly. We have farmers with bins full and cupboards bare and we are talking about a technical amendment to the bill. We should be talking about what is happening world wide in the agricultural community. In Saskatchewan, 4,000 farmers felt that their livelihood was in such jeopardy that they had to abandon all that they normally do at this time of year and protest their conditions. We in this House and those who are in a position to make a decision should make one that is favourable to the fabric of Canada and the livelihood of the farming community. We should stand up and take notice.
We are polite. Our tone is muted. We are talking about jobs. We are talking about livelihood and a way of life. We are talking about a farming community that is slowly but surely being eroded before our very eyes. We are talking about families who can no longer plan for a livelihood within a family with respect to a profession that was both noble and useful.
I was at the International Ploughing Contest a couple of weeks ago. There was a very important button that I saw with a slogan. It said: "No support, no farmers, no food." We are talking here as if this is again an academic exercise. When we talk about food shortage world wide, who in heaven's name is going to produce while we sit back and watch our farmers disintegrate before our veiy eyes as their industry collapses because "You know, we were going to have a discussion on technical purposes of this bill."
October 8, 1991

I do not mean to diminish the interest of the House or the interest of the government, or the minister. Most of our members here are quite aware of what is going on in the agricultural community.
I am speaking from the view of an Ontario member, one from an urban environment such as the city of Toronto. It is almost criminal that we can point to retail prices for food products that have escalated dramatically upward over the course of the last 10 years while farm gate prices have remained at the same level that they were at the beginning of the last decade.
We can talk very politely about bushels of wheat being at the same price in absolute nominal dollars as they were a decade ago. It is just insane. It is just insane. We expect our farmers to maintain not only their way of life but an annual production, improve their quality, make themselves more efficient and make Canada much more aggressive in world sales of a much needed product.
We do not do that in the industrial sector. One of my colleagues from Broadview-Greenwood in Toronto was the first to tell us in this House that one of the things that happens in the industrial sector is bang, bottom line, out we go, because we are not making the dollar.
We are essentially asking people in the farming community and in the agricultural community to subsidize a very luxurious way of life for us. We are paying top dollar at the retail level for some food products while the farmer at the farm gate is getting what he was getting 10 years ago.
If I take a look at what has just happened in my own province of Ontario, farm income projections for this year indicate that the net farm income for Ontario will have declined by 27 per cent in the last four years. Twenty-seven per cent. Imagine maintaining an industrial enterprise with those kinds of figures, knowing that at the same time during the same period interest costs and operating costs have increased by 15 per cent.
On the one hand we have interest expenses increasing by 15 per cent over four years and net income decreasing by 27 per cent. It is no wonder that the farming community is in chaos, total chaos. We have high quality wheat, international prices that are low, and no sales or relatively little. We are talking about one major deficiency. One of the problems that my colleague from Algoma has pointed out is that we have not really
Government Orders
addressed the implications of the free trade agreement and its impact on the agricultural industry. We have noted that there is a subsidy war, a trade war, between the United States and Europe and who is getting caught in the crossfire? Our agricultural community in Canada and most of all those of us who are consumers.
We have not looked at the implications of the free trade agreement when it comes to subsidies. We are supposed to eliminate tariffs on profits. I thought and the general impression I dare say among most members in this House is that subsidies that would be deemed unfair would not be applied. Yet we have the United States artificially maintaining a low price for many of our agricultural products, preventing our farmers from being able to sell a product on the world stage that will bring great benefit to Canada.
In fact again, for Ontario and Ontario alone, with total farm cash receipts of over $5.6 billion annually, we are not talking about an insignificant industry. In fact it is so important that agriculture in Ontario alone generates a further $17 billion a year for the Ontario economy. Seventeen billion dollars. That is similar to the total amount of money that is spent in the province of Ontario for health benefits.
Can you imagine what would happen if that kind of industry were allowed to go in the direction where it appears to be going, thanks to our lethargy. For those of us who are concerned about jobs and employment, I hasten to remind everybody that the agricultural business and associated business provide 12 per cent of all jobs available in Ontario.
Can we sit idly by and allow that pool of job creation opportunities to lapse and to collapse? We sit here with courtesy, with appropriate demeanour. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, I am shocked. I am shocked that we have not seen Canadians-maybe this is characteristic of the way that we deal with things as Canadians- out here at the front of the Commons ensuring that we pass legislation. My hon. colleague who spoke before me suggests we account for kinds of expenditures that go for the benefit of our citizens. If we do not spend our money for the benefit of our citizens and if we do not spend our money to maintain a lifestyle and a quality of life that we hold dear and we say characterizes Canada and all of its inhabitants, for what purpose are we in this place?

Government Orders
We are talking essentially about seeing an integral part of Canadian society being transformed completely.
We are seeing farms abandoned on a daily basis. We are seeing families abandoning a livelihood that has been there for generations and moving to cities. At the same time, we are seeing cities like those of Toronto, specifically Toronto, experiencing an enormous increase in unemployment. There has been a 73 per cent increase in welfare costs over last year and a 50 per cent increase in unemployment since the beginning of this year. We are seeing the collapse of an industrial base that would be required to absorb this enormous migration from rural Canada to urban centres.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that the minister wants to put forward a bill that would allow us to go into the traditional form of sales with the appropriate caution. We have to safeguard, of course, the hard-earned dollars of all Canadians.
I wish that we would be a little more energetic when it comes to selling the product that is second to none in the world and when we come to guaranteeing a livelihood for Canadians who have sweated by dint of their brows to ensure that we are vigorous and productive world-wide.
I do not really want to say much more. What is happening is that we are getting very high retail prices for a product that is very, very good and we are recognized as being a very efficient producer, but we are providing our producers with very little. We seem to be taking a secondary position to some of the more aggressive nations in the world when it comes to selling our products.
Mr. Speaker, I know you want me to finish but if you would give me a moment, I just want to refer to some statistics of destinations of Canadian agricultural exports coming from Canada's trade in agricultural products in 1986, 1987 and 1988. It shows, for example, that we have had a precipitous decline in our agricultural products everywhere around the world, most specifically in the United States. We can see why with the artificiality of the low cost of their products.
We see an enormous decline in exports to developing countries. The only place where we seem to be holding our own is Japan. To the EEC, thanks again to this trade
subsidy war that we are engaged in with the United States, we are going downhill.
What is required, Mr. Speaker, is not just simply minor amendments and technical bills. What is required is an aggressive action by this government, its agencies and the Canadian Wheat Board to sell the products that our producers have so diligently and so properly put together and provided for the marketplace and for consumers world wide.
We owe it, Mr. Speaker, not only to ourselves and the agricultural community in Canada but to the world market and all consumers world-wide to be aggressive and dynamic in selling a product that is so purely Canadian.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly appreciate the intervention of the member opposite, especially somebody coming from an urban riding. I agree with him and I think there is a lot of concern out there over the agricultural situation. I would like to just give him a few numbers to help put the issue into perspective.
First of all, the hon. member talks about prices that were as bad as they were 10 years ago. It is even worse than that. Prices are basically the same in some commodities as they were 30 years ago. In fact, if you want to do a direct comparison, the price of wheat now is essentially what it was in 1971, which is 20 years ago. The point he makes is well taken and that is to try and think of a farmer making ends meet or a business operating with today's expenses on the income that he had 20 years ago.
Second, I want to suggest to him that the situation is the same right across the country, whether it is in Ontario, the prairies, the maritimes or Quebec. If it is the grain and oilseeds side of things, prices are very, very bad. There is no question about that.
Third, you talk about the free trade agreement, Mr. Speaker. Members in the House should know that as a result of the free trade agreement, the U.S. is now becoming more and more a customer of Canadian products. The U.S., believe it or not, is the second most non-subsidized market that Canada has. We sold over one million tonnes of all grain and oilseeds to the U.S. in the last crop year. When you think about it, the U.S. is the largest exporter of grain and oilseed products in the

world and yet it is about our fourth or fifth largest customer. So the free trade agreement has provided a more secure access to the U.S. market than we have ever had before. A result of that is that the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board, the Canadian Wheat Board, other agencies and individuals who sell into the U.S. market have done so in increasing amounts. So the free trade agreement has actually helped us in terms of quantity going into the U.S. Also as I said, after Japan it is the second highest market in the world.
When the member is talking about the free trade agreement, he should take some of those things into consideration.
The last thing I wanted to just point out is that he talked about our markets going down. In fact, that is not the case. Canada has maintained its share of markets but we have done so at horrendous costs as far as price is concerned. So we continue to sell.
The reason we do not sell as much to the European Community as we did previously is that it has what is called variable import levies in place that very much keep the Canadian product out of their market. We can be as aggressive as we want but unfortunately there are no trade rules that apply to agriculture products the same as there are for other products. That very much keeps us out of that market.
We are being very aggressive. In fact Canada and the Prime Minister have taken the lead in putting these issues on the table internationally to try to get a resolution to them.
We are not sitting idly by, by any means. The record is there to indicate otherwise.
I want to conclude by agreeing that this is a very serious situation. I intend to say some things at third reading that point out the problem that we have and how absolutely criminal it is in many ways that when the world needs food and we can produce it, prices go down and we see more people going to bed hungry.

I welcome the intervention of the minister who took great pains to agree with some of the statements that I made. I acknowledge that and I thank him very much for understanding that we do have a serious problem. The real value of income coming back into the agricultural community is akin to that which it was 20 years ago, or in some instances 40 and 50 years ago. That
Government Orders
already shows that we have a problem of disastrous proportions.
I have to take some exception to the attempt to correlate a positive component of sales with the free trade agreement. The minister has given us an indication that we have maintained our market share but that does not indicate for the producer in Ontario and Saskatchewan, Alberta and elsewhere that we have actually continued to sell very productively. We have already talked about the value of the sales that we have made in real terms and that value, to all intents and purposes, has gone down. You can maintain a market share all you want if you are not getting the appropriate income from it.
With respect to the United States being a major consumer of our products, that is one of the misfortunes of our marketing strategies. It might be true and it is true that the EEC has some very prohibitive legislation for our products but the EEC is not the only market in the world, nor is the United States.
We have just learned that one of our major flour mills, Ogilvie, is actually importing U.S. wheat for its milling operations. The situation is not as the minister would have us believe that we have secure access to a market in the United States. One of the things that the United States is doing is buying our product knowing that the prices are so low, handling the sales and turning right around and selling the product on the international market.
I can see the minister saying: "Well I cannot believe that that is true." Well, it is true. All he has to do is go down to the brokerage houses in Toronto and he will see what is happening.

I have just a brief comment, Mr. Speaker. I am impressed with the enthusiasm that we are getting from some of the urban members. I wish that more of them would be as interested and supportive in what is happening to their food sources.
I guess because I have been here 11 or 12 years watching with great concern the decline of rural communities that it is not as easy for some of us who live it every day to be as enthusiastic as he was in our presentations. When one is watching the decline of the place where one grew up, and the families one knew, and the problems that your own family is having, it is not easy to become enthusiastic. I appreciate and applaud what he has done

October 8, 1991
Government Orders
today by putting a fresh approach on the humdrum presentation of the facts, and by an acceptance of dealing with the legislation that we have before us.
What we are hoping to do with the quick passage of these two pieces of legislation here today is to make room on the parliamentary agenda for the government to present legislation that will provide a $1.3 billion pay-out to farmers this year, which is the shortfall that exists in net farm income for the 1991 crop year.
We are very enthusiastically awaiting the announcement by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the various ministers responsible for agriculture for that to occur.

Mr. Speaker, my enthusiasm should not be confused with any kind of eagerness. What it should be interpreted as is the kind of energy that is required I think to drive home the point that this is an issue that affects all Canadians. That is where I come from on this. It is not a situation where I am getting enthusiastic because I see farms collapsing on a day-to-day basis. Nor is it one where we see Canadians suffering virtually everywhere in this country.
In fact, it comes from a desire to ensure that a very important component of our social fabric and a very important dimension for the Canadian economy is not only preserved, but is nurtured, maintained and moved forward for the benefit of all Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
I have just a brief comment, Mr. Speaker. The member made reference to Ogilvie importing wheat from the United States. I believe he is talking about a shipment of some 19,000 tonnes. That sounds like it is too much. I forget the number. It may have been 19,000 tonnes. The information I have is the reason Ogilvie did that is because of what happened with the grain inspectors. Because the grain handlers refused to cross the picket line, Canadian supplies were not available.
The member should be a little bit careful when he talks about linking that kind of a purchase which is, as I understand it, a one-time shot simply because Canadian supplies were not available. If he is criticizing that, then he should have been voting for the legislation that put public servants back to work, including the grain inspectors which, if they had stayed at work, would have not meant that Ogilvie had to go outside the country to buy wheat. He should be a little careful when he uses some of that information.
Second, I agree with the member for Mackenzie. I think this kind of support and enthusiasm, and I say enthusiasm in the best possible use of the word, is very helpful as far as having urban people understanding farm issues. I would be very happy to spend some time with the member. I invite him to come to committee and we can air some of these things and he can get a better understanding.
Again, I am not saying that his understanding is not useful, but he could understand fully some of the implications of the trade war and some of the things that we are trying to do to support farmers. I think this kind of support in the House from urban members is very welcome.

Mr. Speaker, I just could not let the minister's comment go unchallenged. The fact of the matter is that Ogilvie with its one shipload, which is a substantial amount of wheat that will have been imported if we accept the minister's calculation, does not come necessarily from the grain inspectors. One of the problems is that we have had an erosion of a transportation system in this country, thanks in large measure to his government's policies over the course of the last seven years that are not permitting us to move grain as efficiently as we need to move it in order to get it to the markets where it is required. That has been the problem. It has not been the legislation that was before the House last week.
