speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. The House is constituted as a committee of the whole to consider Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
Shall clause 1 carry?
On Clause 1-Guarantee [English]

Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of questions to put to the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds.
In the Auditor General's report he suggests that there is some $4.2 billion which is not properly authorized by Parliament. I wonder if the minister could say who the five top largest debtors are, or who owes that money to the Wheat Board. What countries are involved in that?
In the Auditor General's report of 1990, reporting on the fiscal year 1989, the Auditor General suggests that some $3.4 billion of this money is from financially troubled countries. I am not sure if that is a great exclusive club because it seems to me a lot of countries which are supposedly rich countries are also financially troubled countries, including our own. But I am wondering just which countries are in debt to the Canadian Wheat Board.
The Auditor General's report goes on to suggest that the value of the board's troubled receivables is impaired by at least $2.1 billion, and this impairment continues to grow at the rate of $300 million a year.
I am assuming that that word "impairment" might better mean that they are not able to repay at all, or are incapable of repaying, since it is suggesting that some $300 million a year is added to the account or the debt. I wonder if the minister could tell us just which countries owe the $2.1 billion that appears not to be able to be repaid, and whether the government is planning to write that off, or whether it just continues to build up at the rate of $300 million. In fact, it was suggested by the hon. member for Mackenzie that the $4.2 billion that was in the Auditor General's report for 1990 had grown to $4.6 billion.
What we are trying to do is to give legal authority for new shipments of grain that are bought on credit by
Government Orders
countries and by individuals around the world. We are trying to give legal authority to the existing debt. I wonder if the minister could tell us about those details.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the member's first question of who owes the Canadian Wheat Board money as a result of credit sales, I am sure the member will know that this is a very competitive market and what goes on as far as transactions is very sensitive and, therefore, is commercially confidential. We make every effort to comply with customer's concerns, even over the price that a sale has taken place for, for an appropriate period of time.
For me to stand in my place and signal to everybody, because this is full public record, who is owing money to the Canadian Wheat Board would not at all be appropriate and I do not think would be very useful. In fact, it would be very destructive to the board in its sales efforts.
With regard to the rescheduling and what the Auditor General says there, I made the point with the member for Mackenzie previously, that again we consider all of the debts as being sovereign because the Canadian Wheat Board signs agreements backed by central banks and governments of countries that we do business with. Therefore, from our point of view, if it is a sovereign debt it is ultimately repayable.
On the occasion when there is rescheduling that takes place, and there is a standstill, and we give countries breathing space, and a judgment call is made, then that is handled differently. That is put on the books in a different way. But until some of that rescheduling takes place, then the amount outstanding, because it is sovereign with other countries, is considered fully collectable.
The last point the member asked about is the rescheduling. If one looks at page 43 of the annual report, again it is not appropriate at all for anybody to talk about which countries are rescheduling, but there is a number there toward the right hand side of the page at the bottom. As of July 31, 1990, total rescheduling amounted to $3.3 billion, including $1.25 billion which is the Canadian equivalent of $1.8 billion receivable in United States funds.

October 8, 1991
Government Orders
In terms of countries, again it is a very difficult thing to do because we in no way want to impair the Canadian Wheat Board's ability to sell based on information that would not be useful in a commercial relationship. The numbers are there in terms of the total amount. If the member wants to turn to page 48, again as I pointed out to the member for Mackenzie, there is a listing which could be considered contingent liabilities. It is up from $3.7 billion in the previous crop year to $4.6 billion as of the crop year ended a year ago. The annual report for the just concluded crop year is in preparation. It will not likely be available for, I would think, another month to six weeks.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has the annual report open. Perhaps he could put on the record the amount of federal monies that went to the Wheat Board account by way of interest that was not paid by the defaulting countries that was paid into the account so that the farmers and the board were not responsible for those losses.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
I am wrong when I say that the report will be available. It is not available until some time, I believe, in February or March. I just wanted to correct that.
Again, it is not appropriate. If we were to put that kind of information out it would be very simple to calculate from the interest back to what the principle would be. If the member wants to look at page 43, there is a list of the various countries the board does provide credit to.
Just so that we use the right words, I am not so sure that "default" is the right word. As I said, because the debts that are incurred, or the loans that are made, are to sovereign countries and they are considered, therefore, as part of a country's sovereign commitment, we consider them collectable until they are rescheduled. So, I am not so sure that the member should use the word "default."

For clarification then, were there any funds that went from the Government of Canada to the Canadian Wheat Board account in lieu of either interest missed or debts not paid in any of the past years and if so, what would that amount be?
I am not asking for commercial information. I am simply asking something that taxpayers and members of Parliament should be aware of. Flow many tax dollars
did go to the Canadian Wheat Board, if any, to pay for either interest or loans that had not been kept up to date so that the farmers or the Wheat Board did not have to carry that liability?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Let me try to explain it this way if I can. It is simply that when you think about transferring money from the Government of Canada to the Wheat Board to the farmers, that is not really what we are talking about here.
When the board makes a sale, if in fact the people who they are selling to do not pay fully, it goes to the market and borrows money.
We put a bill through the House, the hon. member will remember, about three or four years ago to give the board better opportunity to operate on the market. It can now issue its own paper in Canada and the United States. It is expanded to credit unions, trust companies and the whole thing. The member will be aware of that.
The board then decides how it is going to raise the money. It does so on a sovereign guarantee from the Government of Canada. If in fact that country or that individual cannot repay, the board has to keep borrowing. As the interest piles up or increases, the government guarantee just increases with that.
To suggest that the Government of Canada pays money into an account as a result of interest accruing on debts that have not been satisfied is not the right way to think about it.
If the member is talking about money on a deficit in the pool account for which the board has not been paid, then there is provision in the act that the government pays interest. I think the member will know what I am referring to there.
There have been cases when there has been a deficit in the pool account. Because the board has not received the full amount of money from its purchaser, the government pays interest from the end of the crop year for an appropriate period of time to satisfy that requirement so that the producers are not out.
Again, I do not think it is right to say that the Government of Canada actually puts money into a Canadian Wheat Board account to satisfy interest as a result of a customer not paying its loan when they anticipated they would be able to.
October 8, 1991

Perhaps the minister or his officials could explain the impact of the amendment to section 33 of the act. It refers on the second page to the principal so guaranteed and any interest that accrues during that pool period with respect to sales of wheat on credit, et cetera.
The guarantee of the interest was part of the act before this change. That was why I was curious as to whether any payments had in fact been made under that particular portion of the act that has been in existence for the last two or three years, or whether this is simply something anticipating a situation.
From what the minister has been telling us, apparently there has been no transfer of funds to pay interest foregone or interest that could not be paid and that is really all I need to know if that is in fact what he was telling us.
There has not been any requirement for money to move from the Government of Canada to the Wheat Board under this particular section of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that is precisely my understanding of it.
What simply happens is that the line of credit or the credit limit simply gets raised to take into account the amount of interest that has to be paid by somebody to keep that loan outstanding.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to make some comments on this bill today. I must say that I am very much in support of the amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act that would allow the government to authorize the Minister of Finance to make these payments.
As I indicated earlier this day, every piece of legislation has to be amended from time to time. In that context, I think there has been an oversight here and I want to propose a very simple technical amendment that requires the addition of two words to correct a huge error that was made a little over a year and a half ago.
I am sure in the minister's own mind he realizes the blunder that was made in early 1989 when oats were removed from under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. We all know that the price of oats plummeted shortly after the decision was made and the price never recovered.
Of course the positive impact I believe for the minister himself, because I am aware of the criticism levelled at him when this was removed from under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board, is that this amendment would ensure that such a mistake would never happen again. If such a move had to be passed by this House, we in the Liberal Party would never allow it to happen.
So this removes the government discretion and makes this inclusion mandatory that these grains are included in the act itself. Therefore, I move:
That Bill C-23 be amended by adding thereto the following clause: "3.18(2) of this act is repealed and the following substituted therefor: 3.18(2) Except as directed by the Governor in Council, the Board shall not buy grain other than wheat, oats and barley."
I move this amendment, Mr. Chairman, seconded by the hon. member for Algoma.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The Chair takes under advisement the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex.
It being one o'clock, shall I rise, report progress and request leave to consider the bill again later this day?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

It being one o'clock p.m., I now leave the Chair until two o'clock p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, 20 years ago today multiculturalism became official Canadian policy. It came alive here in the House of Commons. Then Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau christened it with these words:
"A policy of multiculturalism commends itself to the government as the most suitable means of assuring the cultural freedom of Canadians-National unity, if it is to mean anything in the deeply personal sense, must be

October 8, 1991
founded on confidence in one's own individual identity; out of this can grow respect for that of others and a willingness to share-"
Indeed, multiculturalism as a policy affirms that "freedom to be ourselves cannot be left to chance."
Canada is home to all who have chosen to live here. The people of many cultures have built this country. The nation is living, breathing and always changing.
It was in Canada's interests that this House proclaimed multiculturalism as an instrument of national unity 20 years ago today. It is in Canada's interests that today this House reaffirm its commitment to multiculturalism. National unity may depend upon it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Haitian community, I wish to thank and congratulate our Prime Minister for his firmness in defending rights and democracy in Haiti.
The thanks of the Haitian community also go to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his courage and determination and to the Minister for External Relations for her firm stand.
Many organizations, associations and friends of the Haitian community in Quebec and Canada have assured me that they would never forget this remarkable stand our government took to restore democracy in Haiti, despite some difficulties.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian AIDS Society has declared this to be AIDS Awareness Week. The theme across Canada is AIDS: Our Challenge for Life.
If the government's original response to this challenge, the National AIDS Strategy, announced in June 1990 is to succeed, there must be more funding and support. The organizations in Canada working to control and reverse the AIDS epidemic are having to deal with increasing numbers of cases without a corresponding increase in funding. Even the current limited and increasingly inadequate federal commitment will end on March 31, 1993.
Mr. Speaker, AIDS is not the disease of the 1980s. It is still with us in the 1990s and the crisis is far from over. We must increase resources and extend our commitment to fight this terrible disease, as the Ontario government announced yesterday it will do.
I am certain the persons living with AIDS and their loved ones in this country and those who have died already as a result of this disease are looking to us for concrete evidence of our understanding that AIDS does indeed pose our challenge for life.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to a company that continues to show leadership in waste control.
Friday, October 4, marked the 10th anniversary of Laidlaw Waste Systems blue box program. Laidlaw currently recycles 40,000 tonnes of household and commercial recyclables per year. The anniversary was celebrated with the opening of a 10,000 square foot expansion to Laidlaw's Mississauga facility, establishing it as the most innovative recycling plant in North America.
When the Laidlaw blue box program started 10 years ago in Kitchener, the company collected three products for recycling; newspaper, glass and cans. Building on the success of the original program, Laidlaw now recycles 12 products through its Mississauga facility including corrugated cardboard, glossy magazines, household plastics, textiles, and white goods such as fridges, stoves and their associated CFC gases.
I want to congratulate this private sector firm for working hand in hand with governments in accepting the responsibility of preserving our environment and at the same time preventing the wasteful use of our natural resources.

Mr. Speaker, this past weekend members of the Company of Young Canadians held their 25th reunion. CYC volunteers from across the country convened to discuss those very
October 8, 1991

special creative years and to share insight into current social problems which plague our country.
The CYC was brought into existence through legislation to encourage young people to share their energy with communities across the country which faced grave social and economic challenges. Training sessions in community development and human relations enabled these same young people to contribute greatly to the communities sense that they deserved a say in decisions that affected their lives and that the sound principle of participatory democracy was indeed a principle to be upheld and respected.
These same volunteers voiced sincere concern that today young people do not have in place a similar opportunity to serve their country. They also reaffirmed their ongoing concern and commitment to continuing to contribute to and assist in promoting the principles of community development and concern for their fellow citizen.
I bow to and honour these CYC volunteers who remain as energetic and caring today, 25 years later.

[Translation)

subtopic: STATEMENTS MADE BY FORMER PRIME MINISTER PIERRE ELLIOTT TRUDEAU

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENTS MADE BY FORMER PRIME MINISTER PIERRE ELLIOTT TRUDEAU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of a minority, I feel I must comment on the statement made by the former Liberal Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau. A statement of this kind by a man who has an international reputation and enjoys a certain credibility is unworthy, irresponsible and libellous. I would even call it psychological terrorism, an attempt to intimidate those who are seeking a country that is tolerant.
Minorities are full-fledged Quebecers and are treated as such by all Francophone Quebecers. Distinct society or not, minorities have nothing to fear. As far as scare tactics are concerned, Quebecers were exposed to worse during the seventies under the Trudeau government.
It is high time someone told him: "Put your feet up, Grandpa".

Mr. Speaker, when the treasury board president announced that top level government appointees would receive big fat bonuses at Christmas while all other public servants would get nothing, not even a lump of coal, my phone rang off the hook. And all of this on the coat-tails of the largest back to work order in Canadian history.
For the record, here is what some of my constituents had to say: "You should demand that the treasury board president resign". "I didn't picket before but if they went out again I would be on the line". "I am outraged at the blatant display of political shenanigans". "I am disgusted".
Mr. Speaker, I share these opinions. This is a government run amok. Let us call a spade a spade. The rules of fair play have not been applied here. When will the government realize that if you do not pay Peter you cannot reward Paul. The minister responsible for Treasury Board should resign.

Mr. Speaker, this month marks the 62nd anniversary of the Persons case. In that connection I am privileged to rise today to extend my congratulations to a member of my constituency, Ms. Doris Anderson, who is a recipient of this year's Governor General's Award in Commemoration of the Persons case.
Ms. Anderson has been at the forefront of the women's movement in Canada for more than 30 years and has distinguished herself as a journalist, author and equal rights activist. Perhaps best known as the long-time editor of Chatelaine magazine, she has also served as President of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women and President of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. She has also played a major role in the movement to entrench equality rights for women in the Constitution.

October 8, 1991
Through her work she has made innumerable contributions to the advancement of women in this country and I ask all members of this House to commend her on this important award.

Mr. Speaker, across Canada, farmers are facing extreme economic hardship. For a variety of reasons beyond their control, many farm commodity prices are below the costs of production. Many are being forced to sell their farms or go bankrupt.
Canadians must understand the importance of farming to our national well-being. We in Canada, compared to all other nations, pay the second lowest portion of our income on food purchases, yet we complain. The fact is that if we in Canada lose our ability to feed ourselves, we will end up paying whatever the hand that feeds us demands: our cash, our natural resources, our political support.
Farming is also vital to our Canadian economy in terms of trade revenues and its spin-off support to supply, handling and processing industries. Farming supports the rural lifestyle preferred by so many Canadians.
In my riding of Northumberland and across Canada, farmers demand that this government commit to defending and improving the viability of the whole Canadian agricultural industry at the upcoming GATT negotiations. In particular Article XI of GATT must be clarified and strengthened to protect our supply managed producers.

Mr. Speaker, over the weekend the member for Willowdale, who is the Liberal industry critic, was at a conference in Toronto and was a cheerleader for a free trade agreement with Mexico.
The spokesman for the Liberal Party is quoted as saying that this is a marvellous opportunity to amend the free trade agreement. How naive, Mr. Speaker. The Liberal Party should recognize the fact that the present trade deal has cost over 200,000 jobs and that a further trade deal with Mexico is a more massive threat to Canadian workers.
Why are the Liberals waffling? Are they seeking to regain the financial support of the large corporations which are sponsors of the free trade deal? Now is the time to stand against the free trade deal. It is not the time to be tricked and trapped by the Prime Minister and his corporate friends who want a corporate agenda for all of North America.

Mr. Speaker, according to the Minister for International Trade, Mr. Wilson, a proposal to update the Constitution and improve market efficiencies within the country does not go far enough to solve the problems facing the Canadian economy.
A close examination of the Canadian economy would support this position. For example, between 1985 and 1990 unit labour costs in the U.S. declined marginally whereas in Canada they climbed 48 per cent. As well, wages in Canada have increased 27.6 per cent compared to 18.6 per cent in the U.S.
In response to these realities, the Minister for International Trade will embark upon a prosperity and competitiveness campaign. We look forward to the minister's prosperity initiative as we face the realities of a global marketplace. As it is often said, Mr. Speaker, there is no place left to hide.

Mr. Speaker, I attended a meeting of over 500 farmers in my riding in Nova Scotia on Friday concerning the general picture of agriculture. They have an understandable concern about western wheat and/or the wheat war and that our international trade negotiators might forget Article XI of GATT.
I want to take the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to impress upon the government, especially the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Agriculture, that while there is the understandable concern about western wheat, that in the negotiations under GATT going on in Geneva now, there can be no back-peddling on the position we put forward December, 1990 on Article XI of GATT. Any change would be a disaster for
October 8, 1991

supply management and would affect so many farmers in other parts of the country than the west.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to draw your attention to the Environmental Choice Program and its first national consumer awareness campaign.
Environmental Choice was created by the Prime Minister and the Government of Canada in June 1988 to provide consumers with environmentally responsible alternatives in the marketplace.
Since its creation the program has come a long way. Today its symbol of certification can be found on more than 500 products and services of some 80 companies. These range from re-refined lubricating oil to residential composting systems and diaper services, and the list grows every week.
The awareness campaign is designed to reach out to Canadians across the country through television and print messages. It will help consumers more easily identify products and services that are less harmful to the environment. It will also help industry recognize the market advantages enjoyed by products and services that bear the program's certification.
I ask that Canadians take note of this important program. Only with their widespread involvement can Environmental Choice make a significant impact.

Mr. Speaker, there are people who say Quebec's sovereignty will cause a flight of investment capital. We must realize that capital moves for various reasons: interest rates, availability of labour, market conditions, technological change, and so forth.
The government's financial position also has an impact on the movement of capital. Political instability will also affect this movement.
Today, foreign capital is avoiding and even leaving Canada, mainly because of the deficit and also because of political instability.
In Quebec, we know what we want. We want to get rid of federal bad management. We want to get rid of political instability, in order to build a prosperous Quebec.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the financial farm crisis which exists in western Canada today is the worst in recent memory.
With farm gate prices slashed to early 1970 levels, grain producers are unable to pay their operating loans let alone meet their long-term debt obligations. Consequently there is an immense amount of pessimism in the region, the most severe in fact that I have ever seen.
As our grain producers have a genuine and immediate need for financial assistance, I was pleased to be present in Winnipeg last Friday when the Prime Minister promised the third line of defence committee that additional federal dollars would soon be forthcoming.
However, western grain producers and the businesses that support them are also dependent on those who move the grain to market. That is why striking grain handlers at Thunder Bay must be legislated back to work. Moreover, grain handling must be declared an essential service so that farmers will never again be the innocent victims of highly destructive strikes as they have been this autumn.
The farmer's plight is extremely severe and we must respond immediately.

Mr. Speaker, the time has come to get serious about job training in Canada. At a time when companies are warning our government that new jobs will materialize only if we can generate enough skilled and educated people to use the latest technology, our response to this challenge has been unacceptable.
Federal expenditures on training as a share of the GDP have fallen from .19 per cent to .17 per cent during the period 1987 to 1990.

Oral Questions
On the job training is outrageously inadequate. In 1988 the average worker in Japan received 200 hours of training. In Sweden, 170 and in Canada, less than 7 hours.
At a time when we have a 30 per cent high school dropout rate, I urge business, government and labour to devise a strategy and to co-operate so that we can have an effective and dynamic training program for our youth, our workers.
The federal government must take the lead.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Some 50,000 farmers, or one out of every five farmers in Canada, are in danger of losing their farms.
Nowhere is the situation more desperate than in Saskatchewan, but the Prime Minister seems to be waiting for just the right moment in the Saskatchewan election before announcing an emergency aid package.
When is he going to stop playing politics with the lives of farmers? Why does he not announce an emergency aid package for western farmers right away?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend would seem to suggest that our interest in western agriculture has just begun. A point of fact, in the seven years that this government has been in office we have increased assistance to western agriculture by 650 per cent from the levels left by the Liberals.
We have tried, as best as any government can, to stand with the farmers. I met in Winnipeg with the representatives of the third line of defence. I pointed out to some people after that in 1962 when I was private secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, which is 29 years ago, the question then was $2 wheat and the question today is $2 wheat, some 29 years later. This means that everything else has gone up and the farmers' prices have remained stable at 30-year old levels. This is unacceptable.
The Government of Canada has stood with the farmers before and we will stand with them again.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the Prime Minister that my interest with the farmers of western Canada goes back to my grandfather who was a farmer in Alberta and goes back to all my uncles who have been farming in Saskatchewan and Alberta, so it is not new for me to talk about farming in western Canada.
What we see happening today seems very familiar. Everyone knows that during the last Saskatchewan election the Prime Minister was able to find a billion dollars just at the right time.
I want to ask the Prime Minister: Is he waiting for another midnight call from Grant Devine, who will be defeated anyway?
The farmers of Canada cannot afford to wait. The farmers of Canada want action right away. Why does he not do what has to be done right away?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know, unlike my hon. friend, who will be elected in Saskatchewan at the election. That will be the decision of the people of Saskatchewan. The problems of the farmers of western Canada are unrelated to any electoral results. They are related to justice and well-being. This government has stood with them in the past and will stand with them again.
We are moving as quickly as we can. As I indicated last Friday in Winnipeg, I instructed the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture to try and bring together, within a week, a specific proposal that we would then share with the members of the third line of defence committee, which is the way we have been working with them since last spring. That process seemed to meet with fine favour among all the representatives who were there from across Canada. I think it is a reasonable and appropriate way to proceed, in co-operation with the provinces and in co-operation with the pools and producers, and that is what we are trying to do.
With regard to my friend's grandfather from western Canada, he is one of our strong supporters.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not only are this government's agricultural policies destroying the foundations of Western Canada's economy, but this very day, conservative economist
October 8, 1991

Thomas Courchene said that Canada was in danger of disappearing as a result of high interest rates and an overvalued dollar.
Why does the Prime Minister not act immediately to make Canadian goods more competitive abroad and bring the dollar down to a normal level so that our workers can find employment throughout the country?

Mr. Speaker, interest rates have fallen nearly 6 points in almost a year. For the past three months, inflation has been below 3 per cent and we are aiming for a rate of 3 per cent next year. Economic growth is expected to be
3.5	per cent next year.
So I think that the government's economic strategies are working fairly well, considering that the IMF just said that economic growth in Canada would rival Japan's next year for the lead of all major industrialized countries. The record is not so bad.
Now if my friend, a former Minister of Finance and President of the Treasury Board, is telling us that the Department of Finance should give the Bank of Canada a directive to lower the value of the Canadian dollar artificially to 80 cents, let him say so directly, because he knows the immediate disastrous consequences for Canadian investments; he knows that the inflationary impact in Canada would be catastrophic. What will help lower the value of the dollar are falling interest rates, rising growth rates and prudent management of public affairs, which we are doing.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday, Thomas Courchene who is director of the School of Policy Studies at Queen's and an advisor to this government, told the Canadian Exporters Association that high interest rates and the overvalued dollar are creating "a reserve army of the unemployed".
I ask the Prime Minister: Why will the government not cease now those policies that are conscripting 1.5 million Canadian workers against their will into its reserve army
Oral Questions
of the unemployed? Why does this government insist on leading them in a death march to economic oblivion?
Mr. Speaker, we are following a course of economic development that my hon. friend can-
It is not working.

My hon. friend from Willowdale says it is not working.
Ten years ago this morning, when his government was in office, the interest rate was 20 per cent. Today it is 8.75. Inflation ten years ago this morning was 12.6 per cent and rising. This morning it is 5.8 per cent and declining. That is the program of this government.
We are not going to return to that kind of philosophy. It does not work. We have inflation that is dropping. We have investment that is increasing and we have the economy on track for what the OECD says will be impressive economic growth in 1992 and 1993. I think that is good news for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said that the economy is on track, but Professor Courchene told the Canadian Exporters yesterday: "Our overvalued Canadian dollar is hollowing us out all along the production, tourism, cross-border shopping spectrum". "Moreover", he said, "our monetary stance is imperilling our future". That is a strange way to keep the economy on track, to take steps that will imperil our future.
I ask the Prime Minister: Will he cease those policies now that are imperilling our future and bring back hope to the Canadian people about their economy and their future?

Mr. Speaker, there is an alternative to the course that we are following, that is the course pursued by my hon. friend when he was President of the Treasury Board where spending in Canada increased by 14 per cent a year every year for 15 years. During that period of time the debt in Canada increased by 1,100 per cent. That is a lethal course for Canada and we are not going to follow it.
Deindustrialize Canada.

My hon. friend from Willowdale yells his favourite word "deindustrialize". A point of fact, since the free trade agreement was brought in, the net inflow of foreign investment in Canada, positive invest-

Oral Questions
ment in Canada, was some $4 billion. For the first time in 15 years there is that kind of net investment flow into Canada creating the new jobs that Canadians need.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister is aware of the absolutely desperate situation among prairie farmers. In a way it is very difficult even to describe the tension, the stress, the problems with families, the suicide rate and such things in the rural prairies.
In view of the fact that farm income now on the prairies is less than one-quarter of the rate of the national poverty level in this country, I wonder if the Prime Minister can level with the House today and assure us that when he makes this announcement there will be an emergency package of more than $1 billion for farmers in this country. Can he tell us exactly when that payment is going to be made?
Families out there are really under stress. They need an answer and they need it now.

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in Winnipeg, even though the Government of Canada does not have the money, we are going to try to find the money as quickly as we can to put together a package that will help the farmers who are affected by this crushing drop in commodity prices.
As I speak, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds are putting together a proposal for cabinet which I believe will come forward on Thursday. As quickly as I can thereafter I will be happy to advise my hon. friend.
We are trying to help the western farmers in every way we can. I know, in keeping with that, he would want to help the farmers by asking his friends in organized labour to cease that work stoppage in the Lakehead which is stopping the sale of western wheat.

Mr. Speaker, our party has been asking for mediation in that dispute now for a long time. We have been trying to get both sides back together. The Minister of Labour is fully aware of our endeavours.
What I want to ask the Prime Minister is: Why can he not announce that package today? He has known of the problems now for many months, in fact going back six or eight months. The situation has not changed. It is desperate on the prairies. Why the delay? Does the delay have to do with Grant Devine's election schedule? If so, why this cynicism? Why not announce it now? Why play games with people's lives, is what I am asking?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend knows that we have put together the GRIP and NISA programs which will be putting, within the next eight months but as of September, some $2.5 billion into the pockets of Canadian farmers.
What we are talking about is a deficiency payment over and above that to meet the shortfall on income that affects individual farmers across the country but principally in western Canada.
This is something that was dealt with by the third line of defence which brought together people from across western Canada. I met with them on Friday. We had a lengthy and productive meeting. All of the people representing the family farms, the pools and so on across the prairies seem to think that the way we are proceeding is the right way and the productive way.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals seem to find this funny, laughing at the opinions of the western farmers, but I can tell you that I think the farmers will welcome the prudent, thoughtful and I hope generous manner in which we are proceeding.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister.
I do not think that farm women who bear intolerable burdens because of the poverty, the insecurity and the stress in their lives and the lives of their families will feel
October 8, 1991

that the approach this government is taking in delaying so long any kind of emergency help is the right way.
I want to ask the Prime Minister: How does he think that families can manage on $6,300 net income and feed their families? When will the government make a commitment and pay these emergency funds that families are waiting for and desperately need?

Mr. Speaker, I understand, I think, very well the concerns in rural Canada, not just in western Canada but in Ontario, Atlantic Canada and Quebec. What we have been doing is working with the farm leaders in that area to bring about whatever assistance we can as a government in Canada. That means that we will have to, as the Prime Minister said, use every resource to address the need.
What we have to do, though, is understand that there was an announcement last summer of some $543 million that flowed. There will be another $1.5 billion that will flow before Christmas and $1.1 billion will flow after.
That being said, it still does not bring a return to the producers of grains and oilseeds in Canada any higher than the return they got 29 years ago in 1962.
We are going to be able to address it. I hope the opposition will support every piece of legislation and every necessity that this government puts forward to support agriculture, including helping to settle the strike at Thunder Bay which is harming agriculture in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Canadian farmers are facing the worst financial crisis in a generation because the government cut support programs by $1.3 billion and has not provided any cash assistance this year so far.
The Minister of Finance has aggravated the situation because of his high dollar policy which is costing Canadian farmers over $400 million a year. When is the Minister of Finance going to help Canadian farmers? When is he going to lower the value of the Canadian dollar?

Mr. Speaker, I do not quite understand the rationale for the question from my Liberal friend.
Oral Questions
How are we going to lower the dollar? Is he suggesting that we arbitrarily set the price of the dollar? Are we going to say the price of the dollar is now 75 cents or 80 cents? Is that what they are suggesting?
I do not have a background in economics, but anybody who does thinks that that is an absolute asinine way to run an economy in a country.
As far as the assistance to agriculture is concerned, the hon. member knows that we have been working with the established groups. We have been working very hard over the last two years, first of all, to put in safety net programs and, second, to address the stupidity of the international grain war with the Americans and the European community. They are really, really carrying out a ridiculous war and harming Canadian, Australian, New Zealand and other farmers. Third, we are looking at ways of supporting the market. We are looking at ways of supporting our agricultural producers by allowing others who need our products the opportunity to buy them.
This takes some time, but I would say to the hon. member that the crop year that we are talking about is still under way. Com is still being harvested in Ontario and grains and oilseeds have just been completed in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, every one of the farm established groups told this minister and told the government last spring that it needed at least $1.3 billion of emergency cash assistance last spring. The government has not provided one cent of that money.
After the Rosetown rally of over 3,000 protesting farmers last week, the minister said that he had no intention of providing emergency assistance to Canadian farmers. Last Friday the Prime Minister said that there is going to be aid. I want to know: Who is telling the truth?

Mr. Speaker, the western Canadian, the Ontario and the Atlantic farmers know who is telling the truth.
They know who has been beside them since 1984. They know who has increased agriculture spending. They also know the assistance they got from his government when interest rates were 24 per cent and when farms were being foreclosed.

October 8, 1991
Oral Questions
This government, since 1984, has assisted agriculture 650 times more than his government did. I say to the hon. member: When I was asked in Saskatchewan about aid being provided, whether there would be $1 billion for the province of Saskatchewan alone, I said: "No, that was ridiculous".

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Minister of Finance.
A recent study of our oil and gas sector said: "The appreciation of the Canadian dollar since 1985 has cost the producing industry a total of about $3.5 billion in lost revenue".
Our farm, pulp and paper, mining and other resource sectors have been devastated by the dollar which has gone up since 1985 successively. Many jobs have been lost. Farms have been lost. Which one of the options available to the Minister of Finance does he intend to take to bring the dollar down?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to hear from that side of the House the talk of high dollar.
Back in 1978 the dollar was at about 87.5 cents and today we are seeing interest rates at a much lower rate than back in those days. That is what we are trying to do: get inflation down, get interest rates down, and keep them down. That will allow our people to be more competitive.
I might remind the hon. member of a quote of Dennis Williams, chairman of General Electric Canada: "A lower dollar might make everybody's life a lot easier, but it is not the difference between winning and losing".

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister. The pulp and paper industry in Quebec, and of course in the other provinces, is in danger. Hundreds of jobs have been lost in recent weeks because the Canadian dollar is overvalued. Will the Minister of Finance finally listen to all
participants in the economy and bring down the value of the Canadian dollar?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think, in the example that the hon. member gave in the pulp and paper industry, he knows full well that there is an oversupply in that particular industry at the present time and it is a competitive position.
Most economists will tell us here in Canada that it is not the high dollar where we are having our major problem. Where we are having it is in our lack of competitiveness. It does not have to do with the high dollar, but in fact they talk about the labour costs in manufacturing which have increased in this country by 28 per cent while our productivity has only risen 1.2 per cent.
For our major competitor, the United States, in the same period of time salaries went up 18.2 per cent, but at the same time its productivity went up 18.6 per cent. We have to be more productive in this country and that is why the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology is working so hard on this area with his colleagues and with the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in fact the person that we have been talking about throughout this Question Period, Thomas Courchene, professor of economic and financial policy at Queen's University, as well as a previous adviser to this government. He has said that the Canadian dollar and its increase has cost Canada two-thirds of our competitiveness against the United States.
Given this very strong criticism and given that Mr. Courchene has been a key adviser to the government in the past, will this government accept his recommendation to lower the dollar to 80 cents and cut interest rates to help our exporters right across Canada?

October 8, 1991

During that time we did not get more competitive. We saw our standard of living slip.
If we look around the world today to the Japanese and the Germans, they have the strongest currencies. They have the strongest economies. I think the hon. member has to reflect on the fact that the level of the Canadian dollar is but one element of competitive position. If we only focus on that we are going to miss the boat because there are other elements of competitive composition such as the amount of research and development that is spent by industry, the amount of training that is done in the country, the amount of investment that goes into improving the productivity of companies, the competitiveness of our domestic market, and our ability to sell internationally into other markets in the world.
It is that combination which allows-
It is time to move on. The hon. member for Essex-Windsor will put his supplementary question.

Mr. Speaker, the minister talks about these other areas, but the failure of this government in those other areas has been just as great as the failure with respect to the high dollar policy.
Does the government not realize that it is time for it to act, or is it just going to let John Crow continue to run his high interest, high dollar policy until the economy of this country is completely ruined?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister concerning the very critical situation in Yugoslavia.
The British Foreign Secretary this morning said that the European community has done all that it could to bring about a cease-fire in that country and has now asked the United Nations to intervene directly.
I want to ask the Prime Minister: What specific measures Canada will take today to help put an end to the bloodshed in Yugoslavia and to protect the people in Croatia?

Mr. Speaker, the position adopted by the European community today in regard to the United Nations is a position that the Government of Canada put forward to the Secretary-General of the United Nations exactly 10 days ago.
We believed at that time that this truce was unlikely to hold and as a result we felt it imperative that the Security Council be seized of this matter and that a peacekeeping force be invited in. Canada was ready to be part of that and I signalled that to the Secretary-General.
We believe that this would be a beneficial presence, as it has been around the world. There is no reason whatsoever for young Serbs and Croats to be dying in the interests of 18th century nationalism in Europe. That is a situation where the United Nations can intervene and can be helpful.
I thank the Prime Minister for the answer.

Barbara McDougall, our Secretary of State for External Affairs, who was there, representing with great dignity and courage the interests of the Government of Canada.
Hear, hear.

Today, at the United Nations and through the Organization of American States, we are pursuing various peaceful solutions. Why have these executives been receiving bonuses of up to 25 per cent of their salaries since 1987 without public disclosure to the people who are footing the bill, the people of Canada?

Oh, oh.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me repeat for perhaps the seventh or eighth or tenth time in the last few days that for the pay period
October 8, 1991

commencing after the budget of last spring the bonuses will be zero per cent.
Let me repeat again the invitation I make to the hon. member, his party, or anybody else: If they can come up with a better, fairer way of establishing a remuneration for heads of agencies, Crown corporations and so on that will be fair to the taxpayers, that will ensure that the persons are remunerated based on what the rest of the economy gets, we wait for that suggestion.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to come back to the Croatian issue and ask a question of the Prime Minister.
In view of the June referendum in Croatia in which 94 per cent approved independence, reaffirmed last night by a declaration of Croatian independence, and in view of the continuing violence by the Yugoslavian army in Croatia in addition to the measures already referred to in this House by the Prime Minister involving the Security Council of the United Nations in peacekeeping, will the government show leadership on this issue, first, by again strongly condemning the violence by the Yugoslavian army; second, by insisting that the Yugoslavian army withdraw from Croatia; and, third, will the government today commit itself to back up those measures with tough economic sanctions in concert with the European community?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with my hon. friend in one important area. The Yugoslav army is absolutely out of control and has caused extraordinary damage both to the Serbs and the Croats in Yugoslavia who have lived for some four or five decades in a state of peace and economic growth and prosperity in that country.
With regard to the question that he raised, on October 4 I wrote again-I think it was the third or fourth time-to the President of the Republic of Serbia and to the President of the Republic of Croatia making
Oral Questions
precisely and in the strongest possible language the points my hon. friend has raised.
In regard to the fundamental issue, the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated yesterday that Canada believes that the twin track approach agreed to on October 4 is the most realistic way to solve the crisis. This agreement provides for those republics that wish it to gain recognition in a framework of a general negotiated settlement that would protect minority rights, ensure against unilateral and forcible changes of borders, and provide for a loose association or alliance of sovereign republics.
This is consistent with everything that previous governments have stated in regard to a problem of this nature, and it is a case that we have vigorously made at the United Nations Security Council.
We are going to try again, both at the Security Council and with our colleagues in Europe, to make sure that there is an intervention because the violence and the killing in Yugoslavia must cease.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Prime Minister for the answer and ask a supplementary question.
The Croatian community in Canada, as well as other members of Parliament including the member for Bur-naby

Kingsway, have been urging the government to move immediately on humanitarian assistance in Croatia, particularly in food and medicine.
Will the Prime Minister now advise the House that the government will move on humanitarian assistance routed through an independent Slovenia direct to the people of Croatia?

Mr. Speaker, we have been in touch with the leaders of both the Serbian and Croatian communities in Canada. We have already committed humanitarian assistance to these peoples, and Canada is prepared to do more.
The edicts of the European community and the expression of will of the United Nations Security Council must be heeded. There is no reason whatsoever for sane men and women to tolerate a situation where an army is absolutely out of control and bringing death and destruction to an otherwise quite prosperous nation that was struggling for unity.
We hope that the intervention of the United Nations and/or the economic community will bring the parties together so that both Serbs and Croats can realize that

October 8, 1991

their destiny can be a peaceful and a productive one together.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
Last night on the CBC news, former employees of Nationair charged the airline with very serious safety violations.
We also learned, and I have a copy of the document, that for the very first time in aviation history a safety review of the airline was ordered by Transport Canada two weeks after a DC-8 Nationair crashed in Saudi Arabia on July 11, which killed 247 passengers including 14 Canadians.
I ask the minister: In light of the evidence presented last evening, will the minister immediately make public the findings of this special review so as to reassure Canadians and the travelling public that Nationair is safe to fly?

Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying that Nationair is safe to fly. It has been complying with all recommendations that have been made occasionally by Transport Canada.
I think the member knows that the airline industry around the world is in very big difficulty. I do not think that allegations of this kind are profitable to Nationair or to any other industry, because Canada is still the country with the best safety record in the air.

Mr. Speaker, the minister obviously did not hear my question because I made no such allegation.
Now that the allegations of former employees of Nationair are in the public domain, given that his own department for the very first time in aviation history has issued a safety review, given the fact that he has said that Nationair is safe, and I am happy to hear that, and given the fact that a review has been put in place by this government, can the minister release those findings so as to reassure Canadians that what he has said today in the House is backed up by facts and information issued by his own department?

Mr. Speaker, I repeat that all recommendations which have ever been made by Transport Canada regarding Nationair or other airlines are always very scrupulously followed. We make sure that they have been corrected. Every time we receive a direct complaint from an employee, we keep the records confidential. It helps anyone who wants to make a complaint to do it in all confidence that the information will not be revealed and therefore he or she can be very open in their comments.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The House again in Committee of the Whole to consider Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

When the committee was interrupted at one o'clock p.m., clause 1 of the bill was under consideration. When the committee rose, the Chair took the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex under advisement.
According to citation 698 of the sixth edition of Beauchesne, an amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant or beyond the scope of the bill. Bill C-23 seeks to amend only two sections of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, sections 19 and subsection 33.(1).
The proposed amendment reaches back into the parent act and seeks to amend section 18. Accordingly the Chair must find that the proposed amendment goes beyond the scope of the bill and is out of order.
Resuming debate on clause 1.
On clause 1-

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to put a couple of more questions to the minister. I must say in passing that it is unfortunate that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex was ruled out of order. It is unfortunate because it really represents the wishes of the vast majority of prairie grain producers.
The producers were appalled. There were votes by the Wheat Board Advisory Committee pummelling the
minister. He has hardly recovered from it since, because he took oats away from the Wheat Board. It is a pity that the amendment is beyond the scope of the bill because I think even the minister, in retrospect, would say to himself and this House that he regrets having taken oats away from the Wheat Board.
Mr. Speaker, all you have to do is look at the annual report of the Wheat Board for 1989-1990 and you will see that when the minister took it away, he also took away the assistance that was available to those wheat and oat producers. You can see in 1989 the assistance available was some $26 million for oats and $2,688 million for designated oats.
Even the minister, if he could be totally candid here today and of course he carries the responsibility of office with him so he has difficulty doing that, would say it is a pity that oats and barley are not under the Wheat Board Act as the motion from the hon. member proposed.
The minister said he could not reveal what the debts of individual countries are. I recall when Lech Walesa was here and met with the standing committee on external affairs, a question was put to him by, I believe, the hon. member from Edmonton on our side of the House. He asked him what could be done that would assist Poland. This was at a time when it was going through a return to democracy. He replied that one of the greatest things would be if the government could forgo those debts for, I believe, $1 billion or $2 billion for wheat and food aid.
In view of that, I wonder if the minister can indicate a couple of things to me. First, have the Canadian Wheat Board and the Government of Canada actually forgiven any of the money owing under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. It would be interesting to know just which countries have been given that forgiveness. I would be interested especially to know in view of the representations made by the Prime Minister of Poland if the government did move on that recommendation or that suggestion. That was my first question.
My second question is this. I wonder if the minister today could indicate to the House the exact magnitude of the wheat pool account deficit for the crop year 1990-91 completed on July 31. I wonder if the minister could indicate the amount of that deficit. I note that in the
October 8, 1991

annual report one of the countries that obviously owes some of the $4.6 billion owed to the Canadian Wheat Board is Haiti. Has aid been cut off to Haiti because of the military coup which occurred there a couple of weeks ago and because of the decision by the Organization of American States to impose certain economic sanctions against that country? Could the minister respond to these three questions, including my question as to whether or not he still agrees that it is wise to have oats included under the Canadian Wheat Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I get quite a large charge out of the hon. member and the oats issue. This is really a red herring. I stand by the decision and there are all kinds of people in the industry who support that decision. In fact the hon. member should have been with me a week ago last Friday when I had the pleasure to cut the ribbon at a new oats processing facility in Portage la Prairie. It has the potential to process, once they are up to full capacity, something like 80,000 tonnes of oats annually. Now 80,000 tonnes may not mean a lot, but put it in this kind of context. There were years in the past when total exports out of Canada for all oats did not exceed 100,000 tonnes. Eighty thousand tonnes is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 20 per cent of the total production in Manitoba.
The significant thing about the announcement was that the president of the operation called Can-Oat Milling Products Incorporated said at the opening ceremony that there were primarily two reasons why this plant was being built, in addition to the transportation facilities and the quality of oats they could purchase in the area. First was the free trade agreement because they had better and more secure access to the American market and upward of 80 per cent of the product is going to move out of the country.
The second thing he said that made it more feasible was the fact that they could go out and contract directly and have more control over the raw product that they buy to make their various forms of oat products from.
For him to suggest that we are rethinking the oats decision is nonsense. He said I was going to have difficulty being candid. I am being very candid. I do not have difficulty in speaking about what I believe in. If he wants to be straightforward he should look at the drop in price of oats since, let us say, the crop year beginning August 1, 1989, which is a little over two years ago and compare it to wheat. He is going to find that in
Government Orders
percentage terms wheat has dropped more. To suggest that because oats was taken away from the Wheat Board there has been a big drop in prices and that is the sole reason is absolute nonsense. If he wants to be more than candid, if he wants to be straightforward and do the arithmetic he will find out that is the case.
The other point I want to make is that oats on a volume basis was half of 1 per cent of the board's operations. That is how much it was. I think it was their 11th or 14th most important product as far as exports from the country, and by value it was probably closer to one-quarter per cent of what the board did. To suggest that oats has been a major crop and that it is causing all kinds of problems as far as producers are concerned is absolute nonsense and he knows that. He is just raising red herrings. We have more important things to talk about here than that. We have some serious problems in the prairies and in the part of the country that the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex represents. We would be better off spending our time talking about how to solve some of those problems than to drag up things like oats.
He mentions Poland. Again, there has been no forgiveness of debt as I understand it. There has been some rescheduling as far as Poland is concerned. It is my understanding, and I could get him further details, that we have also offered them some consideration down the road as far as interest payments are concerned.
Other than that I do not think it is appropriate to comment very much on commercial arrangements. I mentioned that.
He also asked about the Canadian Wheat Board deficit. When the board has all its numbers done and is in a position to announce final payments -and I don't think it is any secret that there is not going to be a final payment in wheat this year-the board will announce all of the numbers. For me to speculate or to announce ahead of time is not appropriate. Starting in 1984 the government, myself namely, stopped announcing final payments. I said: "Look, we are going to announce initial payments because the Government of Canada guarantees initial payment. That is a government decision". When the board goes out and sells, that is as a result of its sales efforts so it announces the final payments. Good or bad, it has announced final payments every year since 1985 and I have no intention of changing that practice- which I would be if I were to announce a deficit prior to

October 8, 1991
Government Orders
all the calculations being done and the board announcing final payments.
If the Canadian Wheat Board uses the same timetable it has in the past, final payments will probably be available right at the end of this calendar year, or at the beginning of 1992.
With regard to Haiti, I don't know that I can say anything more than what has been in the news. I am not totally up to date because I think some of these events are happening almost as we speak. But we have done some business with Haiti. It is my understanding that there has been consideration by the UN of sanctions. I don't know where that is at. But to date, as a result of the unfortunate circumstances in Haiti, I am not aware of anything that we have been doing differently as a result of that situation compared to what we were doing a week or two weeks ago.

A couple of weeks ago the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister paper put forward in a newspaper article done by Carole Gour of The Toronto Star the idea of an international kind of reserve of wheat for food stocks especially designed to assist those republics in Russia that are facing starvation or serious shortfalls this winter. Some observers in the international food aid programs suggest that if there was an international arrangement for wheat reserves for food for starving nations that was well put together, the actual reserves available for cash sales would be very little more than what is adequate for the market around the world. Those reserves have been drawn down, I think to something like 22 or 23 days of supply.
I am wondering whether the Canadian Wheat Board or the minister's department are involved in any of those discussions. Was the parliamentary secretary, who comes from a wheat growing area, only talking in a general way about something that would be highly desirable in the world or was he was flying a trial balloon from the Prime Minister's Office? Just what is happening there? Have there been any discussions by the minister or the Wheat Board with international food agencies as to what kind of arrangements could be initiated? Clearly the situation in the world is pathetic when you look at the amount of reserves there are and the need for food aid assistance
around the world, and then you look at world prices. It is just a disaster that the price of wheat is not at least where it was 10 years ago and not where it is today, which is about less than 40 per cent of where it was some 10 years ago.
I am just wondering if the minister could advise us or is this done entirely by the Department of External Affairs and not by his department. Obviously any serious calculations or international discussions at the end of the day would end up back with the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds and the Canadian Wheat Board. It is after all the agency which would have to provide those supplies and reserves required for some kind of international assistance and food reserve program.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is referring to an article by Carole Goar in The Toronto Star I believe last week. I agree with the member when he says that the situation is absolutely deplorable around the world when you look at food reserves and the fact that we have the capacity to produce. We have all kinds of money being spent on subsidies, and yet more people are having problems feeding themselves. We end up with problems of farmers trying to stay in business. It literally boggles the mind.
We do I believe on a regular basis purchase something like one million tonnes of wheat a year. I do not know how we would compare to other countries but I suspect quite favourably. CIDA through its operations purchases something like a million tonnes of wheat a year, most of it from the Canadian Wheat Board, and some of it from the Ontario Wheat Growers, and other products as well.
There was some concern over Ontario soya beans. They have recently become eligible to supply. We do that. There is also on a voluntary basis the Canadian Food Grains Bank that is headquartered in Winnipeg. There are arrangements made where if a farmer wants to donate a certain number of bushels of wheat it will be matched by the government through CIDA. That is all the grain that is made available as far as development assistance.
Beyond that, again I have to agree with the member that this does not make any sense. I do not know where the member gets the 22 days. I think what he is talking about is 22 per cent of stock to reserve ratio.
October 8, 1991

Having said that, it is still a relatively small number compared to what it has been. It has been up as high as 30 percent, 32 per cent and 33 per cent, and now we are down in the low 20s, but even 20 per cent of 365 days is not much more than two month's grain supply. That is not, by any measure that I am aware of, an excessive amount and one would wonder why prices could not increase with that stock to reserve ratio being as low as it has ever been, maybe even historically.
Beyond that, I do not think the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister was floating a trial balloon. He has had a long-standing interest in this area and has been active himself with the Canadian Food Grains Bank. There have been many suggestions that this should be something that could work.
If one has surplus that one cannot sell, every country has a share that it would put into some kind of a food reserve or a grain reserve. One would have to establish prices going in and establish rules coming out, and establish some kind of criteria for countries to be eligible, and to segregate countries that can afford to pay. Obviously, a country like Japan that is not food self-sufficient is in a much better position to pay than some of the countries in Africa.
Canada was, I like to think, the last country to comply, not only with the spirit but the intent of the last international wheat agreement that really collapsed in the middle 1970s. As a country, we have a pretty good record of trying to work with international organizations to bring about the kinds of things that we are all concerned about here.
We have been looking at almost anything and everything that we can do, bearing in mind the fragility of the GATT negotiations. The member would also be interested in knowing that there is some renewed interest in the International Wheat Council headquartered in London. There are things that I think many of us would like to see happen to the International Wheat Council, that it needs to be more than just a monitoring and a statistical collecting agency and that it should be able to take a more active role in proposing things like the hon. member is suggesting and that the parliamentary secretary has suggested.
Government Orders
In terms of a definite proposal, if there is a total walk away from the table at GATT, and none of us wants to think about it, then with all of these things that we have done some preliminary work on, we are going to have to pursue as many of them as we possibly can to bring some stability back to the international grain market.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not mean to delay the proceedings, but I think the minister must share, at least to some extent, our disappointment in the fact that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex was out of order.

She is being coy.

It would test the whole House.

It would test the whole House, as the hon. member for Algoma says. I think the majority of members, even on the other side, realize that the government made a big blunder. Certainly Canadian farmers do. Apparently the price has gone down continuously since the jurisdiction was removed. Really it could not have been worse.
