I wonder if he would give his consent for that to happen?

Government Orders

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
The hon. member makes a pretty convincing case. Unfortunately I am not so sure he even convinces himself of what he is saying. I appreciate his interest in agricultural matters, but I would suggest that if he wants to talk to the farm community, especially in the Province of Alberta, where the hon. member comes from, that produces, I think, 60 per cent of the oats in the country and about 80 per cent of the oats exported that that is where the decision should be made.
If the hon. member wants to talk about oats, I think he should talk to the producers involved. I would be very happy to take him to the producers who think this is the best thing that could have happened as far as oats is concerned.
There is no question that oats went down in price. I want to suggest to him that barley went down more in price than oats did over the same period of time after it was taken away from the board. Durum wheat went down considerably more in price. Milling wheat went down. They all went down because of international prices.
There have been cases where oats have been selling almost as high a feed barley, which is unheard of. Therefore, it is a pretty sticky wicket for us to get into philosophy on the floor of the House of Commons, when really we should be talking to farmers, which is what we did before we made the decision.
In conclusion, I would also point out that the one co-operative in western Canada that deals right across the prairies, in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Peace River part of British Columbia, voted at their last annual meeting to remove oats from the Canadian Wheat Board. To get up in the House and suggest that there was unanimous opposition to what the government did as far as oats is concerned, is certainly not the case at all. It has been a good decision. It has been well received by producers. The results are there and we stand by the decision.

Mr. Chairman, I am wondering if the minister with his officials would explain to the House what procedure the government goes through in its budget making to annualize the contingent liabilities for each year's budget? How does it arrive at what will be shown as a contingent liability that may cost the government some money for that year? Does it do it
on the basis of what was lost the previous year? How does it present a more or less accurate figure to the House?
The reason I asked this is that in Part III of the agricultural estimates, the Department of Agriculture points out that deficits arising from sales on credit are relatively rare. We had a somewhat different opinion from the Auditor General who shows that on the contrary, over the past few years, according to him, significant payments have had to be made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. He cites 1986-87, where $208 million had to be paid and in 1987-88 more than $113 million. Then there was the interest on a delayed payment which, I presume, was made to the Wheat Board account where the pool account deficit amounting to $33 million for the year 1989-90 was not paid to the board until the following year. While we understand that the payments do go on occasion to cover that account or interest on accounts that the government was a little slow at paying, we know that the farmers are not supposed to be taking a slightly smaller payment because of delays and that the funds themselves are in fact are forthcoming. We know that happens.
How do we have it presented to us for budget purposes when the House approves a budget? Is it done on the basis of contingent liabilities that have proven to be a cost to the Consolidated Revenue Fund in the year before or is there simply an estimate made? If there are estimates, what process goes into the production of that estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will try to answer in two or three ways. First of all, I think there is some misunderstanding concerning contingent liabilities that the board has that are ongoing on behalf of the Government of Canada in deficits in the pool account.
The deficit in the pool account, and there was one I think four years ago of $208 million, $176 million of which was barley, a small one in oats and $23 million in wheat if my memory serves me correctly.
Once the pool period is closed, which is usually some time about now, the end of September or the first part of October-we would have to talk to the board to know exactly- and if there is a deficit, the Government of Canada picks up interest on that deficit until the final payments are made.
October 8, 1991

Government Orders
The producers themselves do not have to take any less money in their final payment as a result of there being a deficit in the pool account, if the hon. member follows me.
If the member is talking about deficits or contingent liabilities, that is money owed to the Canadian Wheat Board by sovereign states, or at least by entities backed by sovereign states. If they are unable to pay, the board just borrows more money against that account for which the Government of Canada backs them. I hope that clarifies the difference between a contingent liability and a deficit.
If the member is asking how do we arrive at a number as far as a contingent liability, I think it is simply a matter of arithmetic. As to how we arrive at the levels of credit that are available to each country, we have a committee of ministers which look at various countries in conjunction with the board, looking at projected sales for a given period of time. Then we establish regular lines of credit that the board is able to use.
It is the same for other non-board commodities. The board works with the Export Development Corporation, EDC. Again, this is not concessional credit. This is commercial credit on reasonable terms. I think the most we have gone, as far as length, is three years.
This review process goes on on an annual basis. It is reviewed regularly each year. If there is a need to adjust for whatever reason, either up or down, throughout that year we have a provision made to have a turnaround quite quickly so that the system itself does not encumber the board, or anyone who is dealing with EDC for that matter, if they have an impending sale for which they need to have some adjustments in their over-all credit.

Mr. Speaker, I was very impressed with the minister's comments with regard to international co-operation. I do not want to even use the words international grains agreement because it has a bad history.
If the GATT agreement falls apart this fall and we do not succeed, it will be a disaster for everyone in every way, both in the supply managed industries and in the grains and oilseeds industry. It seems to me that there has to be room somehow for international co-operation.
In 1983 the price of a barrel of oil was about $2 and the price of a bushel of wheat was around $2. The oil producers around the world organized themselves and they are getting $20 or $23 a barrel for their oil. Canadian farmers and farmers around the world are getting only $2 a bushel, the same as it was almost 20 years ago.
It seems to me that if the GATT negotiations are not successful this fall, we need to look at ways in which we can co-operate in supplying food aid to the nations and peoples around the world, and some way of co-operating among the producers. As the minister has already indicated, we have something like a 22 per cent situation with 30 or 40 days of wheat in the world. I was very encouraged by his comments in that regard.
I hope there will be ongoing discussions in the Wheat Board, External Affairs and CIDA as to what kind of co-operation there could be on aid, perhaps at the international level with the trade ministers, as to what there could be in co-operation.
During the farm financial crisis this summer, one of the issues that has been raised time and time again by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and the wheat, grain and oilseeds producers, the soybean and com producers, has been that they do not have the same level of export credit arrangements that producers in western Canada have under the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
This is a veiy important issue for them. They have to go through the Export Development Corporation or some other agency of government which apparently does not have much flexibility and as much value to them as the Wheat Board has.
Granted, the Wheat Board takes possession. It sells the wheat. It is a much simpler type of situation, but it seems to me that in tight markets and in tight situations such as the one which we are facing now with the cost of production, with the cost of many grains and oilseeds at half or two-thirds the cost of production, that we should be giving every possible tool to these producers in eastern Canada.
I wonder if the minister is looking, since he is the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds for the entire country and not just for the Wheat Board, at improving those techniques and those instruments that are

Government Orders
available for eastern producers in marketing their grain in overseas markets both in terms of credit, forgiveness, flexibility and all the rest.
Has he been able to take any action on the recommendations and the representations made by those five groups in Ontario, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, the commodity council, the com producers, the soybean producers and the Ontario Wheat Growers Association?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member makes a good point with the last point he makes.
We certainly do not want to see one producer in one part of the country treated differently or have an advantage over one in another part of the country simply because of the way things are organized on his behalf.
We have, as far as CIDA criteria, made CIDA aware. It has agreed to use specifications when it tenders for oilseeds so that it can include soybeans and not just canola oil. I think that is a step in the right direction.
I have had a chance to meet with the Ontario Wheat Growers. There have been occasions when it has expressed concern about the matter which the member raises concerning aid. If it has some direct concerns, we will take them up and do the very best we can to address them.
People outside of the Wheat Board area-it would be the same for canola in western Canada and flax, for instance, that were to be exported which were not under the board-make sure where they can that the EDC is as accommodating with non-board sales as the Wheat Board is able to be with board sales as a result of government involvement. Having said that, it is maybe not that easy to accomplish but we have to work at it and make sure that where we can, we see that there is no difference.
I should point out that I remember when we signed a long-term grain sales agreement with Egypt four or five years ago. The Canadian Wheat Board signed it but Egypt had an interest in Ontario wheat. At the ceremony, we had Bob Holmes who was president of the Ontario Wheat Growers at the time, make sure that Egypt knew that while the Wheat Board was signing a long-term grain sales agreement, there was interest in
other parts of the country in selling to Egypt. We had an opportunity to see that the Ontario Wheat Growers were represented at that signing ceremony.
I would also point out that the $150 million line of credit that has been offered to the Soviet Union has been there for some time now. There has been interest in Ontario com as far as that line of credit is concerned and I think that will be the major grain that will be involved in terms of that line of credit. There is an example where Ontario com growers will be able to take advantage of a specific line of credit that again should help producers.
The member makes a good point. Other than offering him and other people in Ontario who are exporting our full co-operation and being as accommodating as possible, I do not know what I could do.
I should point out to the member and I am sure he is aware, that when we assumed office in 1984 one of the first things we did as government was to host a meeting of the five major wheat exporters, namely the United States, the Community, Argentina, Australia and ourselves. We hosted that at Whistler on the west coast. There was a second meeting, a follow-up, that the Americans called. We very much wanted to see if there were ways to co-operate, not to necessarily form a cartel but a way of seeing that if we are going to compete that we do so in a rational basis so that everybody benefits.
I do not think consumers of grain around the world are going to benefit if in fact prices that they pay farmers to produce that product are so low that the farmers go out of business. We very much wanted to continue that dialogue. Unfortunately after the first two meetings, the one that we hosted to get the meetings going in Canada and the one we had in the United States, nobody has seen fit to call another meeting.
One of the things we have been thinking about is to try to get another meeting like that going. I think we are going to have to wait until the GATT process concludes either successfully or unsuccessfully, but I certainly think there are ways in which we can co-operate. One of the things we are going to be encouraging the International Wheat Council to do is to take a more active role and do something other than simply collecting and disseminating statistics. I think it has a role to trying to work with various countries and do the things that the member
October 8, 1991

referred to as far as bringing stability to the international grain market.

On Clause 2-Deductions from Receipts

Mr. Chairman, as I read clause 2, section 33, this will provide authority for the Canadian Wheat Board to close its pool accounts each year and distribute the final payments to producers prior to repayment of the principle and interest owing by the purchasing country.
Does this in any way change the existing arrangement where it was strictly a letter of comfort from the minister, where there was actually no legal authority for the loan guarantee or the parliamentary authority? It seems to me that this is a very crucial part of the whole arrangement for this Bill C-23.
Could the minister comment on that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amendments to section 33 are in one sense connected and in another sense not connected to the letter of comfort. The Auditor General simply said in paragraph 3(12) of his 1990 annual report that the board's practice is to make final payments on sales made during the pooling period or the crop year regardless of whether the grain is sold on credit. His concern was that if the grain had been sold on credit and the credit had not been repaid, there was some question as to the legality for the board to make that sale. All we are doing is amending section 33 to say that once the credit has been provided and the board has made the sale and all the conditions of the sale have been met, including acceptance of the credit provisions and the terms have been agreed to, that the board is then in a position to go ahead and make final payments out of the pool.
This in no way changes the pooling system or the pooling practice. It just satisfies the Auditor General that we are in a position of being able to administer this
Government Orders
section with a better legal foundation and better authority from the House of Commons.

In this arrangement, the credit that the Canadian Wheat Board operates under is charged to the producer up until the moment of the sale. Once the sale takes place, if the whole thing is a credit arrangement, then the credit of the sale from that point forward is charged to the purchasing company or the purchasing government.
Regardless of where the credit is being charged, whether it is being charged back to the producer or being charged to the purchaser, the pool is closed and the funds distributed among the producers in proportion to what they have produced. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, let us just take a hypothetical case. The board has arrived at a price with a customer and they have agreed on the amount of grain and where it is going to be delivered and the customer needs some credit.
The board then goes to the banks, credit unions, trust companies and issues its own paper in order to raise those funds. It does not ask the country or the customer to raise the funds. The board itself borrows the money so that the board can repay the producer for his grain. I hope the hon. member understands me.
There is no question of money not being available to the producer. This amendment provides for a little firmer legal basis for the board to continue the present practice. So it is not a question of any money either going or not going to the producer. It is just a question of having a better legal basis under which to continue present practices.
The Auditor General was concerned that when the board went to banks or to the market to raise money, which it can do now, there was some question as to whether the final payment could be made when payment in full by the customer had not been made.
What we are saying is that as long as the credit is there and the banks have advanced the money to the board to pay the producers and those credit arrangements are in place, the board has a better legal basis on which to operate and continue the present practice.

Mr. Chairman, I have one short question. Because the cost of the debt is spiralling up by $300 million a year so that it is now at $4.6 billion, there must

Government Orders
come a point where the debt is hopeless and is written off.
Clearly, the banks got a sweetheart deal from the government when they were writing off their debts in Latin America. Surely, many of these impoverished countries are hopelessly unable to pay for food. It is like trying to pay for a grocery bill when the food has already been eaten. I am wondering whether the government has any plans to write off these debts. I suppose the Minister of Finance is rather gun shy about doing that because it would show an increase in his deficit, which they are very sensitive about since the government's outstanding debt of the country has doubled in the last five or six years. I am just wondering if it really presents a realistic situation for the Canadian Wheat Board to be carrying deficits of $4.6 billion on annual credit arrangement of 20 or 25 per cent of its sales.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just say again that while the debt shows in the Wheat Board annual report, it is guaranteed by the Crown and therefore it is really not a debt that would be attributable to the Canadian Wheat Board because the government backs it. It means that the Canadian Wheat Board, at the end of the day, is not going to be called on to make that payment. It could not do that because the Wheat Board, outside some asset in its office building and some hopper cars, really does not have any assets.
It is our view that these debts are sovereign. They are owed by sovereign states. They are fully collectable. If in fact there is going to be any rescheduling or, as the member refers to, sweetheart deals, writedowns, standstills, then that would have to be done as part of an over-all rescheduling package I would think involving many countries.
To date the only one that I am aware of-and I think the details are public; we could certainly make them available if the member is interested-is what happened with Poland. There was I believe a standstill on some of the interest down the road but nothing has been, it is my understanding, written off or viewed as uncollectable. It is all looked at as being collectable pending further arrangements.
Just to emphasize again, while it shows up on the board's books as a big number, it is not at the end of the day the kind of money that the Wheat Board itself or the
producers would be involved in. It is the Government of Canada, the taxpayers of the country.
Clause 2 agreed to.

The House resumed from Monday, October 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-18, an act to amend the Income Tkx Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Cultural Property Export and Import Act, the Income Thx Conventions Interpretation Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Canada-Newfoundland Atlantic Accord Implementation Act, the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Resources Accord Implementation Act and certain related acts, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on Bill C-18.
To begin with, this bill is very difficult to read. It is like a telephone book. One would have to be a Philadelphia lawyer to understand most of the language, the way it is written.
However, there are two areas that I want to bring to the attention of the House which I think are of concern to every member of the House. I am referring to those sections which deal with tax credits for individuals who may have a disability.
When the Minister of Finance first revealed his budget earlier this year to the House and to the Canadian public, there were certain provisions made that on the surface would be of great benefit to a number of people who have disabilities. Many of these proposals are welcomed by myself and by those individuals I speak of.
There are a number of changes to the Income Thx Act which certainly need some clarification. At the present time for an individual to qualify for a tax credit or a tax benefit under existing legislation, the definitions are fairly clearly defined by regulation. The new language that the House is considering at the present time is not clear to me. It certainly must not be clear to people who
October 8, 1991

are heavily and directly involved with the disabled community in Canada, some of whom I have spoken to in the last couple of days.
This is very technical and I do not want to bore people, but under section 89, subsection (3), there is a section here that deals with attendant care for individuals who are severely disabled and require an attendant to be with them to offer assistance that may be required.
As I read the initial proposal by the Minister of Finance dealing with this subject, it was my impression that the government had finally listened to presentations that had been made by the House of Commons Standing Committee on the Status of Disabled Persons and then subsequently by a new committee, the House of Commons Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons. For the last 11 years they have been making the argument that the provision of attendant care to a person who requires it is extremely important if we are to assist that individual to participate in the mainstream of Canadian life.
When I read the actual legislation it does not say any such thing. What the legislation appears to talk about is the tax relief that will be given to the attendant and the individual if they travel to a place that is not less than 80 kilometres from the locality where the patient dwells to obtain medical services. That is not what either the disabled community or the standing committee has been arguing for all those years.
The legislation is still addressing the need for attendant care on a medical model. Many of the individuals who have addressed this committee over the years do not suffer from a medical condition. They happen to be disabled. This provision is not going to satisfy the needs from that very large group of Canadians who have that form of disability. That is one area I wanted to bring to your attention.
Another area that gives me great concern is under section 91 of this act. Clause 91 replaces the existing definitions of what constitutes a disability. I will read the section that is being replaced into the record for individuals who may not be able to or cannot get access
Government Orders
to this particular act within the next few days. This is what it says it is replacing, and this is the present definition:
(a)	a person shall be considered to have a severe and prolonged impairment only if by reason thereof he is markedly restricted in his activities of daily living and the impairment has lasted or can reasonably be expected to last for a continuous period of at least 12 months; and
(b)	the Minister may obtain the advice of the Department of National Health and Welfare as to whether a person has a severe and prolonged impairment.
That has worked fairly well over the years, but now it is proposed that we have a new provision to define disability and impairment. I want to read that out for the record. The new section under clause 91 on page 218 of this proposed act reads:
(a)	an impairment is prolonged where it has lasted, or may reasonably be expected to last, for a continuous period of at least 12 months;
(b)	an individual's ability to perform a basic activity of daily living is markedly restricted only where all or substantially all of the time, even with therapy and the use of appropriate devices and medication, the individual is blind or is unable (or requires an inordinate amount of time) to perform a basic activity of daily living;
(c)	a basic activity of daily living in relation to an individual means
(i)	perceiving, thinking and remembering,
(ii)	feeding and dressing oneself,
(iii)	speaking so as to be understood, in a quiet setting, by another
person familiar with the individual,
(iv)	hearing so as to understand, in a quiet setting, another person
familiar with the individual,
(v)	eliminating (bowel or bladder functions), or
(vi)	walking; and
(d)	for greater certainty, no other activity, including working, housekeeping or a social or recreational activity, shall be considered as a basic activity of daily living.
As I read that new definition, that is going to exclude literally thousands of Canadians who have a mental impairment. By "a mental impairment", I am talking about an individual who is developmentally handicapped, who is quite capable of dressing oneself and of communicating with some difficulty in some cases, but primarily able to communicate, having all the employment opportunities in the present models that we have of sheltered workshops. This individual, probably without skilled

October 8, 1991
Government Orders
training of some degree, would not be able to enter what we would normally call the normal work force.
Those individuals who are presently on disability pensions, either under provincial legislation or with assistance from the federal government, would be excluded from being eligible for any relief under the tax regime if this goes into place.
I want to be fair, and as I said in the beginning I am not a lawyer. The wording as it is presently says to me that those individuals who are currently under existing legislation eligible for tax relief will be excluded under this new provision.
I would urge the legislative committee which will be examining this legislation in detail, and I hope will be calling witnesses and allowing them to appear before that committee, to put these sections I have referred to under strict scrutiny.
If we do not, it seems to me that we will be doing a severe injustice to a large number of Canadians who are least able to defend themselves. It seems to me as parliamentarians we have a clear responsibility in that regard. That is to at least lend some assistance to individuals who are least able to help themselves.
Several weeks ago the government introduced with great fanfare something I welcome as an individual who has been involved in issues of concern to the disabled community in Canada for some time. It was a five-year strategy. The strategy in and of itself has been a long time coming and has been welcomed. We are not sure how that strategy will be implemented over the next five-year period, but that is something we can argue about both in committee and in the House.
The point was that the government took an initiative that has been a long time coming.
If that strategy is to be designed to allow and assist disabled individuals to enter the mainstream of Canadian society, these provisions I just referred to in the Income Tax Act are going to negate any improvements that were promised at the beginning of September.
I could take the opportunity and make the argument that a whole number of government initiatives over the last several years have been harmful to the disabled community: cutbacks in the Canada Assistance Plan,
cutbacks in funding for housing programs and cutbacks for post-secondary education.
I could make these arguments, but I will leave that for another time. I do not want to enter into partisan debate because I think it would detract from the arguments I am making about those sections under the Income Tax Act as we see them.
I do not want to take too long and I do not think I have to in order to belabour the argument but I seriously ask the House that when those members on that legislative committee review this legislation, they pay a great deal of attention to those two or three sections which I think are detrimental to the people who we are trying to assist.

Mr. Chairman, while it is certainly not my intention or that of my colleagues to drag this debate out unnecessarily, there are, while we still have a bit of time this afternoon, a few points that I would like to raise.
The bill before us, Bill C-18, does a number of things, some good and some not so good. One of the items that I noticed has to do with some changes for taxation for persons who benefit from the Older Worker Adjustment Program.
Programs for the older worker's adjustment income will become taxable the same way as unemployment insurance income now is. We are aware that we will not change the government's mind on this particular proposal within the bill but a moral argument could be made that some of these people, especially those former employees of Route Canada, some of my own former fellow workers at Kootenay Forest Products in Nelson, British Columbia and others have suffered more than their share already as they have seen their operations close down.
Some of the closures are due to actions of the federal government and others are due to actions of a provincial government. They are not simply decisions within the private sector.
They have suffered more than their share already and, being wage earners, many of them have paid more than their fair share of taxes already. We do have to ask: Why should their income be fully taxed when, for instance, capital gains are only taxed at 75 per cent? In that regard we wonder, if someone who earns $500,000 from capital gains only has to pay the capital gains tax on three-quarters of that amount, then why is it that a long-time worker who has seen his operation shut down and has lost his livelihood through no fault of his own and gets a
October 8, 1991

meagre $100 or $200 extra a month in pension benefits as a result of the Older Worker Adjustment Income Plan is taxed on the basis of 100 per cent of those earnings? There does not seem to be much equity there.
There are two ways we can look at the matter of taxation. One is the tax system and tax changes themselves, and the other is some of the things that the government spends its money on. I found it rather interesting, at a time when the government and the finance minister are talking about the need for restraint and additional tax measures in order to pay for the operations of government, that we have some of the kind of spending going on that still continues.
I refer now to an item that was in today's Quorum from The Montreal Gazette of October 8. The headline is:
Taxing Subject Matter
In time of government restraint, how much do we need to know about eunuchs in imperial China?
It is datelined Ottawa. It reads:
At a time when the government is paring services, it is spending $15,435 to finance a study on eunuchs in imperial China, with special focus on the 10th to 14th centuries.
That makes it even more vitally important if you look at the timeframe.
It says:
As it is freezing public service salaries, the government is spending $305,070 toward its continuing financial backing of a private project to assemble a dictionary of old English, or rather, auld English.
Among other projects Canadians are helping finance through taxes like the GST are a study of the modern American diet ($27,700), an analysis of criminality and religious charity in 16th century Bologna-
That is really vital to the welfare of the Canadian taxpayers.
-and a look at the late prehistoric archaeology of the Ha'apai
Islands in the Kingdom of Tonga ($80,318).
These are just a few of 680 scholarly projects supported in the fiscal year 1990-91 by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada funded by this government. That agency, created under the Secretary of State Department in 1977, handed out some $82
Government Orders
million in 1990-91 which is up from $75 million the year before.
The president of the agency says:
-the federal spending squeeze meant 473 projects worthy of support had to be turned down.
That is really a shame. I wonder about those kinds of projects. At this time of fiscal restraint and when the government is imposing new taxes on Canadians, what are the gems that we missed out on in the last little while?
These are some of the spending priorities that this government obviously has and at the same time it is making some other tax changes.
I want to refer back to one that makes these other ones seem rather minuscule because this one has to do with forgiving perhaps billions of dollars of revenue from some of the richest families in Canada.
The finance minister would have us believe that he scrounged around to find every possible source of funds that could possibly be put toward deficit reduction. I am quoting at some length here from an article in The Globe and Mail from last March 13:
But few Canadians are aware that just before his deficit-slashing
budget last month, Mr. Wilson's own department quietly gave up a
source of potentially billions of dollars that were scheduled to come
into the national treasury beginning in the next 21 months.
This change does not appear in the bill currently before us, but we are expecting it momentarily. The government has suggested that it is coming. In many ways this is a major measure of tax forgiveness to the wealthiest families in Canada, which it has been attempting to sneak through over the Canadian people at the same time that we have a cap on social spending arrangements with the provinces and people on welfare and social assistance and small children are not getting enough to eat. This assistance which cities across Canada are dependent upon and many other vital programs all members have agreed are vitally necessary for the welfare of the people of Canada but are being cut back and slashed.
The Public Service on which we depend for the delivery of many of our programs is being told that it will get zero and zero, unless its members are willing to give up either their jobs or the jobs of their fellow employees.

Government Orders
Coming back to this matter of changes dealing with private trusts:
The money would have come from the richest families in the country as part of an overhaul of the tax system worked out two decades ago. It would have come from the private trusts of these families-storage places for great wealth that are almost entirely shielded from the public eye.
While considerable information is publicly available about the income and assets of individuals and public corporations, almost nothing is known about these private trusts. So, although the owners of the private trusts have long known that they would owe major taxes starting in 1993, the general public was unaware.
Not surprisingly then, nobody paid much attention on February 11, 1991, when the finance department issued a dull press release No. 91-018 about some seemingly technical matters dealing with family trusts.
I want to go on a bit, because it is about time that some people realized just how this government is taking them for a ride.
Behind the technical language, release No. 91-018, in fact, announced the government's intention to introduce a generous new loophole that would allow the deferral of a fortune in taxes.
Only two weeks later the then Finance Minister was on his feet in the House of Commons declaring an all out assault on the deficit. While many Canadians listened apprehensively to the minister's speech, the owners of the private trusts undoubtedly breathed a little easier knowing that although times may be tough, the government had at least spared them.
The story behind this press release and the action it refers to begins back in 1972 when the Liberal government of Pierre Trudeau introduced some fairly sweeping reforms to the tax system.
One of the items was the removal of the federal inheritance tax. That action resulted in a lump sum gift of about $12.5 billion to rich families, according to calculations by University of Toronto economist, John Bossons.
The extent of this windfall for the wealthy was actually far greater over time, since it removed the inheritance tax on future accumulations of wealth, including the enormous increase in private fortunes in Canada during the 1980s.
To partially offset this loss of revenue, the government introduced, as part of the 1972 reform, a partial tax on capital gains, a key source of income for the very richest among Canadians.
Up until 1972, capital gains, that is the profits made on the sale of assets, such as stocks, bonds, jewellery or real estate, had been tax free.
Although the Royal Commission on Taxation had recommended in the late 1960s that capital gains be taxed at the rate as other income, the government apparently viewed this as too punitive for the well to do and opted instead to tax capital gains at only half the rate applied to other income.
Now who says our governments have not had a heart?
This was a Liberal government and it is known to have a heart. This is the kind of heart it had. Now this Conservative government wants to make the matter even worse and extend these same privileges for another 21 years.
The other special treatment capital gains were to receive was that they would only be taxed when the asset was sold. Its owner could hold onto it for 50 years or more as its value increased, but no tax would be paid until it was actually sold. Stocks could be passed from one generation to the next, thereby permanently avoiding tax
To prevent huge family fortunes from permanently avoiding tax in this way, the 1972 reform package specified that any increase in the value of an individual's capital property would be taxed as capital gains at his or her death, whether or not the property was actually sold.
But private trusts seemed to provide a nice escape clause. By putting assets into a private trust which never died, they would not be taxed when their owner expired.
The Trudeau government set a time limit of 21 years on this. At the 21-year mark, any increase in the value of assets held in the trust would be subject to tax as capital gains. So, Mr. Speaker, justice would finally prevail. That 21-year mark, though, was coming due on January 1, 1993, just in time to provide some badly needed revenue for the federal government's deficit-ridden coffers.
The government, however, created a new loophole that would allow family trusts to put off the payment date well beyond 1993. Proposed in the aforesaid press release No. 91-018, the loophole allows wealthy families in almost every case to choose to put off payment until their youngest child dies, delaying taxes for another generation or more.
Tax experts generally agree that a dollar of tax deferred is a dollar of tax saved. It amounts to tax exemption, because the money saved, if properly invested in the intervening years, multiplies in value.
Release No. 91-018, for all its dry, technical jargon, is the government's signal to wealthy families that it intends to give them an enormous gift. It has done this in a very furtive manner.
October 8, 1991

It chose, for instance, not to announce the change in the budget. A change of this magnitude would usually be announced and some estimate of the lost revenue would be provided.
The finance department has resorted to some specious arguments. For instance, it says in its press release that the 21-year rule might interfere with trusts established by parents for the benefit of their disabled children. How many wealthy families happen to have disabled children? Undoubtedly a small fraction.
And those families who do would undoubtedly have structured a trust differently to provide the child with an ongoing income rather than a lump sum capital gain at a point far into the future.
The government says its new rule will prevent assets from being transferred from one trust to another tax-free. This is a red herring, however, since other tax laws already prevent such tax-free transfers.
Considering the seriousness with which the Conservative government views the deficit, it could have toughened the rules on family trusts instead of easing them.
Canada could have followed the example of its free trade partner, the United States, which is not known for being tough on the rich. But it has tougher laws about this sort of thing than Canada does.
Some time in the very near future, Mr. Speaker, we expect the government will try to pass its proposed new change quietly into law. It will present the change to the House of Commons in the form of a legislated amendment and hope that the few MPs and members of the public which will be watching will have little awareness of the money at stake.
And then, of course, it will return to the pressing matter of reducing the deficit.
I said that the bill now before us does not contain the provisions outlined in the government's press release 91-018 but we do know it is on the government's agenda. I would, ask those members opposite: how can they possibly justify some of the increases in taxation on ordinary Canadians, who already pay more than their fair share, which are proposed in this legislation and in the budget and all of the other measures this government has brought before us, at the same time as they are quietly prepared to hand out billions and billions of dollars to the very richest Canadian families. We are not
Government Orders
talking about those who are well off, we are talking about the super-rich in this society. Why do they need charity when permanently laid-off workers who receive meagre benefits from the Unemployed Workers Adjustment Program need to have an increase in their taxation as a result of this bill before us.
It is socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor, as some people have called it. That is exactly what it is. I do not expect this government to have a change of heart, but I do wish it would stop smiling about the deceit which it has been peddling to Canadians about the sacrifices that ordinary Canadians have to make, while the richest among our citizenry continue to get billion-dollar handouts from this government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West-Revelstoke speak and rewrite taxation history in Canada in his very colourful way. He certainly explained his views of Canada's tax structure and the way it has evolved in the last 25 years in a very thorough and all encompassing manner.
I want to solicit his views on a particular issue. He talked about the evils of the capital gains tax and the way that former governments had applied that tax. As he indicated, and he is quite correct in this, the government at the time imposed a tax on only half of capital gains. In other words, half the capital gains earned by an individual were exempt from any form of tax. They previously had been completely exempt. One of the other exemptions that the government of the day made was to exempt one's principal residence from the application of the tax.

Private Members' Business
None of these was particularly recommended as I recall by the Carter commission whose slogan was: "A buck is a buck is a buck", and proposed taxation on all dollars however earned. He seemed to imply in his remarks that he supported the Carter commission in its report.
Does the hon. member advocate taxation of capital gains on principal residences as part of the policy? Is that part of the New Democratic Party's program for revamping the taxation structure in Canada? And does he take the view that only the wealthy own homes in Canada, only the very rich, the most select few who pay capital gains tax, which again he implied in his remarks? If so, I suggest that his view is misleading and deceptive to Canadians.
I would like him to become clear and tell the House whether or not he supports the imposition of a tax on the gains realized on the sale of one's principal residence.

The answer briefly stated, Mr. Speaker, would be no, not unless there are very serious restrictions on the amounts involved.
What we are talking about here, and going back to the Carter commission, is the need for a fair taxation system in Canada and a taxation system which is seen to be fair. It can be argued in many circumstances, because it is not a perfect world, that there is a need for exemptions from certain types of taxation in specific circumstances to meet a whole variety of very important personal and collective societal needs.
What we say is wrong is when we have a taxation system that again and again and again accords understanding and sympathy to the richest among us when we are not prepared as a government-at least that government and often the government that preceded it-to show that same kind of understanding, sympathy, common sense, equity and sense of fairness to the poorest among us or those average Canadians who work hard and already pay more than their fair share which the Carter commission well catalogued and which many members on all sides of this House catalogued again and again and again.
Let us have some equity, let us have some fairness and treat those who are in the middle and those who are the poorest at least as well as we treat proportionately those who are at the top of the income ladder in this society.

October 8, 1991

He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the privilege of leading off the debate in this House on a Private Members' Bill which I sponsored and whose purpose is to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
As you may know, Mr. Speaker, section 14 of the Act prevents people who are obliged to perform their civic duty, for instance as members of a jury of members of emergency teams, from receiving unemployment insurance benefits if they happen to be unemployed.
I am sure you will agree this is absolutely unfair and that many people are caught in a bind in such cases. Mr. Speaker, I think this section contradicts the intent of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Thiis legislation was passed more than 50 years ago to provide income security for all Canadians, not to punish them when they have to perform their civic duty.

The object of Bill C-211 is to amend section 14 of the Unemployment Insurance Act to ensure that persons in temporary service to the community, as jurors or emergency workers, are not regarded as disqualified from a benefit merely because of their participation in such an activity.
At present, anyone performing their civic duty while collecting unemployment insurance benefits is penalized by the federal government for no valid or obvious reason. Anyone performing jury duty for more than two days will not be eligible for benefits since the law considers that they are not available for work. Although jurors are usually granted a stipend for expenses incurred while performing their duties, anyone submitting unemployment insurance claim cards to receive the difference in UI benefits will receive nothing. I guess to explain it a little better I will refer back to an individual case in my riding that I am quite well aware of that made the media quite extensively in Atlantic Canada. It came to my attention because it involved a constituent of mine.
At that time that I was referred to this case I thought it was a misunderstanding and so did the person in question. We came to find out that the regulation is in fact there. The best way of explaining it, Mr. Speaker, is to read this letter which I received from my constituent that
Private Members' Business
she also forwarded to members of the media in the form of a letter to the editor. It says:
Dear Sir,
In September I experienced the luck of having been laid off after paying maximum unemployment insurance premiums for the past 25 years.
In November I experienced the luck of having been selected as a juror for the murder trial recently held in Campbellton. The mental stress of trying to absorb nine days of testimony and summations was emotionally draining.
The added stress I would also assume is that she was on unemployment insurance benefits, or so she thought and obviously at a reduced salary with no work and not able to look for work.
I am sure that if she knew she was not eligible for UI, her stress level would probably have been that much higher. I quote again from her letter:
At the conclusion of the trial I requested and was given a letter which stated the days I had been present in court and the amount of money that I would receive from the court. I mailed this letter along with the UI card on November 27.
In December I received a letter from the Unemployment Insurance Commission informing me that I was disqualified from unemployment insurance benefits for the two weeks in question as I had not been available for work.
I immediately telephoned the letter-writer to register my disbelief only to be told that I had not been available for work and that there were no exceptions for jurors.
She goes on to state:
My tax money helped pay the salaries of the participants in this case, including the RCMP, the prosecution staff, the public defender, the sheriff's department, the court staff, and not to mention the room and board of the prisoner in question.
In retrospect I could have ignored the summons to appear for jury selection and I would have been fined $50 like the dozen or so other good citizens who failed to show up. I could have requested a letter to be sent to the court by a sympathetic doctor exempting me. I could have lied and said I knew someone connected to the case. I could have lied on my UI claim. Someone suggested that anyone showing up for jury selection with a rope thrown over her shoulder would probably be rejected by the defence team.
However, I did none of these things. I tried to be a good citizen, but I have come to the conclusion that when dealing with big brother honesty is really not the best policy.
That puts it in a nutshell, Mr. Speaker. Basically the person was on UI, was receiving benefits after being laid off employment, and did her civic duty by appearing on the jury.

Private Members' Business
To further matters I have a news article on a situation that happened in Nova Scotia, a little different situation, mind you. I would like to quote from this article and then comment on it. The headline on this article which appeared in The Moncton Times in transcript February 1991 says: "Judge Excuses Potential Jurors, Calls UI Rule 'Stupid'". The by line on the article is Sydney, Nova Scotia, and goes on to say:
A Nova Scotia Supreme Court justice excused nine people from
jury duty TUesday because they would not be available to collect
unemployment benefits if the trial took more than two days.
He goes on to say and this is a direct quote from Justice Hilroy Nathanson:
I think it's a stupid ruling, but who am I?
When we look at who this judge is without looking at the person, but looking at the office that he holds, we see a person who is veiy familiar with justice.
He is very familiar with the legal system and with making sure that people have justice throughout the land. We have this hon. justice saying that this rule is stupid. Obviously, if we go one step further, we would have to say then that it should be changed.
That is why in a way this came to my attention again. After listening to my constituent and seeing this article in the paper, after consulting with my colleagues on all sides of the House, I decided to put forth this bill. I hope that I will have the support today of all my colleagues in the House.
Quite often when private members' bills are presented in the House, government members will come here and try to refute the bills. Quite often they get orders from above. Looking at it in general, I can pretty well predict what they may want to say.
I just want to speak on that for a few moments. First of all, there is a basis principle in UIC. We will probably hear time and time again that to receive unemployment benefits a person must be available for work and must be actively pursuing work.
In the case that we are looking at presently, which is under review and which we hope that this bill will rectify, we find that the lady in question was on UI. She was receiving benefits and decided to do her civic duty. She had no choice. It was not that she had a choice of not being available for work.
Quite often when people are disqualified from UI benefits, it is through an intent of their own to break the regulations. In this case, the lady in question had no choice but to appear for jury duty so she was not available for work through no choice of her own. She was forced to appear for jury duty.
Second, it is kind of hard to pursue employment actively when one is sitting in a jury box. It is very difficult. Obviously she did not meet those two principles. You may hear that from the other side, Mr. Speaker, but when we look at it in a realistic and practical way it was impossible for that woman, that constituent of mine, to meet those two conditions.
Another thing that you may hear is that we are scared to set a precedent. I believe that if you look at the regulations, you will find that precedents have already been set. There are people, Canadians receiving unemployment insurance who are not available for work and who are not actively pursuing work. There are actually some Canadians doing this. It is legal and it is right. There is nothing wrong with that. People do receive sick benefits from UI. They are not available for work, nor are they actively pursuing work. In this case there are precedents involved.
In jury duty we are not talking about a great number of people. Most jurors who appear are already working. We are talking about people who are already on unemployment insurance. We are not talking about people who are unemployed going to jury duty and then getting on unemployment insurance. We are talking about people who are already on unemployment. I would like to mention that.
Another thing I would like to refer to is that you may hear some members today, Mr. Speaker, say-and I hope not-that the justice system, the jury system is a provincial responsibility.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all members of the House that justice is everyone's responsibility. It is everyone's responsibility. I also say that injustices that appear in the system and can be rectified from any level of government should be rectified. In this case there seems to be an injustice done and a further injustice being created by the federal government.
I will try not to be too partisan because I think that in all honesty this bill is a good bill. When you get partisan sometimes, people tend not to want to support you as much. I have no choice but to say that if the government



is saying that it is a provincial responsibility then I think it is shirking its duty. I think it is just passing the buck. In fact, when I mentioned that to a number of my constituents and said I would be speaking today, they actually said: "I find it hard to believe that they are passing the buck because they seem to be collecting as much money as they can get through taxes and just passing on the problems to someone else". That is an opinion shared by a number of Canadians; not necessarily every Canadian, but it is certainly shared by some.
I want to come back to the intent here today, and that is to correct an injustice in the system. It is just a matter of housekeeping. I have talked with a lot of individual MPs and they have told me that it is a good idea. When we talk about private members' hour, the problem is that quite often the government does not want to pass private members' bills. If we look at the record of private members in seeking to pass a bill, we see that is a major problem.
I want to go back and talk a little bit about the Constitution and the new constitutional package which this government wants to promote across the land. A new pamphlet has been put out entitled An Invitation to Help Build a New Canada. That is going to go to every household in Canada, so I am told. On page 6 it says: "We need to make our federal institutions more democratic and more responsive to Canadians. At the heart of the problem is a need for parliamentary reform". I believe all members would agree with that.
It goes on to say: "Many Canadians tune in to televised sittings of the House of Commons, but they are turned off by what they see". They want to see more free votes; that is what they want to see. The government has agreed to that and most members agree that we should have more free votes. That is why I hope we will see later when the vote is taken that it is not just a party vote where maybe the government of the day decides it does not like the bill or it will not get the credit for passing the bill and it has told its members to say this about it, just talk about it, and then at the end vote against it.
I would hope that we would start now with this constitutional package, if it really means something. I would hope that we would set the example. I would hope that members opposite and adjacent would look at the bill for what it is worth and say: "I think it is a good bill. I will vote for it", or "I do not think it is a good bill and I will vote against it". If that is their wish that is no
Private Members' Business
problem, but I would hope that it is an individual desire to vote one way or the other.
I would feel very satisfied with that. I also hope that we would not hear all the government members opposing it just for the sake of opposing it. I believe that is at the root of some of the problem in the land. People have lost a little bit of trust in the system, not in politicians. People tend to equate that with a loss of trust in politicians. If you go to your constituents and talk on a one-to-one basis, there is no problem with politicians as such. It is the system they are complaining about. It is a system like this one where this woman had a problem with UI.
It only makes common sense. If you talk to people they agree with what should happen. They are hoping that members of Parliament who are here today will listen and will improve the system. That is what it is all about. We should start here in private members' hour. In fact that is where the ultimate free vote should always be. It should not matter. We should not even get a declaration from the minister about whether he is for or against. We should just come in here and say: "Let us go to it", and if you agree with it, you agree with it.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I think all members of this House should support my amendment. I think that in this case, partisanship should be relegated to second place and the interests of all Canadians allowed to come first. I therefore urge members of all political parties to support this amendment. The interests of their constituents are at stake.
Since it was created in 1940, our unemployment insurance system has always had equity as its main characteristic. Since section 14 ignores this principle and is basically unfair, it should be amended. Any vote against this bill may very well be perceived as a vote against the interests of Canadians.

I hope that my pleas to reform the unemployment system have not fallen on deaf ears.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration

speechtext:
I wonder if the hon. member could, instead of speaking, open his ears and listen and maybe he will learn something. I was very quiet and listened to the words of my hon. friend across the way. I will be prepared to sit and listen to the words of this hon. gentleman. Perhaps he will just listen to what I have to say.
It is true that people serving on juries are not eligible to receive UI benefits for the time they sit on the jury. This is because they cannot be considered available for work at that time. I will have more to say about that in a brief moment or two.
I would like to point out that it is also true that the fees paid to people for serving on juries in this country are extremely low. For this reason someone receiving UI benefits who serves on a jury is very likely to face financial hardship when he or she is disentitled from UI benefits. But it should also be noted that I do not believe that any judge in the land would ignore a plea to be excused from jury duty when one is seeking employment and on unemployment insurance. That should be underlined.
I have had occasion to be in court rooms when judges will excuse people from jury duty for a number of reasons. If I were unemployed and was called for jury duty and I went before the judge and explained that I was looking for a job and that my UI would be cut off if I had to serve, he would excuse me from jury duty.
Let us briefly explore how the act applies to this question. The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971 was enacted June 23, 1971. Although numerous changes have been made to it, this act forms the basis of the current legislation. Under the act claimants attest to their entitlement to benefits on a bi-weekly reporting card. Here they indicate that they are unemployed, that they are capable of and available for work and unable to find suitable employment. Those are the basic criteria for receiving unemployment insurance.
This process of determining the claimant's eligibility is not limited to when they file their initial or renewal application for benefits but continues throughout the benefit period. Once a benefit period has been established, claimants serve a two-week waiting period before benefits start. Claimants must also show that no conditions or circumstances exist that would disqualify or disentitle that individual from benefits.
UI legislation requires claimants who are receiving regular UI benefits to prove that they are capable of and available for work and that nothing prevents them from immediately accepting any suitable offer of employment. This is really the crux of the matter, and I would repeat that again. The legislation requires claimants who are receiving regular unemployment insurance benefits to prove that they are capable of and available for work and that nothing prevents them from immediately accepting any suitable offer of employment.
This is the test laid out in section 14(a) of the Unemployment Insurance Act. This requirement is mandatory under the legislation and there is no discretion to waive or vary. It imposes on each individual claimant the burden of proving availability for each and every day of employment. The claimants primary preoccupation on a daily basis is to become re-employed. To that end a claimant must be continually seeking work and be immediately available to accept an offer of suitable employment.
If a claimant is unable to accept employment immediately because he or she is serving on a jury there is a strong presumption, I would submit, of non-availability. However, as in all cases availability is evaluated on the individual's circumstances. The decisions will vary according to the particulars of the specific case.

In recent years the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission has developed a policy that permits some flexibility and allows claimants to prove their availability for limited periods of up to two working days in cases such as jury duty, family illness or attendance at a funeral, when claimants would otherwise be able to prove their availability.
This is the most flexible interpretation possible under the legislation which in section 14 requires the individual to be available for work, capable of working and willing to work.
Nevertheless as a general rule a claimant is not considered to be available for work while serving on a jury. The length or uncertainty of the time of duty interferes with the claimant's search for and acceptance of employment.
I would submit that anyone unemployed and looking for a job being called to do jury duty, having a job offered to him and not being able to accept it would be very upset indeed. It goes beyond civic duty.
If jury duty lasts more than two working days in a row, it is difficult for a claimant to claim to be available for work. If arrangements have been made for the claimant to be informed immediately of any opportunity for suitable employment and if it is possible for the claimant to be released and report for work within the following 24 or 48 hours, the claim may be credible.
If in fact the solution to this problem lies not with UI legislation but with provincial judicial systems, generally provincial payments for jury duty are much less than UI benefits. Consequently UI recipients could be penalized for fulfilling their civil obligation.
I agree that people should be compensated for an important function such as jury duty, but the real question is: Who is responsible for compensating them? Is it the employer and the workers themselves or is it the judicial system, as I would submit, of each individual province? I would argue that since they are serving the provincial systems it is their responsibility to provide adequate compensation.
I am going to review very briefly for the House what the provinces are paying for jury duty. Prince Edward Island pays its jurists $40 a day from the first day of jury
Private Members' Business
duty. The average duration of jury duty is seven days in that province. Nova Scotia pays $15 a day from the first day. The average duration of jury duty is three days. New Brunswick pays no fees for the first nine days and it pays jurors $10 a day in mileage and $25 for a full day after 10 days. Quebec jurors are paid $25 a day for the first 10 days, $40 for the eleventh day on. The average duration of a jury in the Montreal region is seven days. Ontario jurists are paid nothing for the first 10 days of trial. I think those kinds of payments for jury duty are not acceptable and the provinces should address them. Manitoba pays $20 a day for the selection of panel, $30 a day for jury duty. The average duration is five days. Saskatchewan pays $25 a day from fourth day of jury duty in criminal cases and $25 for the first day in civil cases. Jurors in Alberta get $10 a day for days one through five of jury duty, $40 after that. Four days is the average number of days served on a jury. The Northwest Territories pays $25 a day and $40 a day. British Columbia pays $10 a day and $30 a day with a two to three day average.
In conclusion, the primary requirement for entitlement after being unemployed is being available for work. I would submit, and I submit very strongly, that it is not the UI system that we should be attacking or seeking compensation from for the individuals to allow them to serve on jury duty. We should go where the problem lies and that is in the judicial system of each province.
Provinces should take the responsibility that belongs rightfully to them and pay the jurors a decent remuneration for sitting and doing a civic duty.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure to support Bill C-211 which has been put forward by the member for Restigouche.
This bill is cleaning up something that was overlooked when the original act was put in place. We are not suggesting for a moment that it is going to cost the UI fund any more money. We are not asking the federal government to put more money into the fund. It does not put any into it now.
What we are saying is that when people are performing a civic duty they should not be penalized by having their benefits cut off, thereby not only putting them under undue stress but also their families.

Private Members' Business
A lot has been said about people serving on jury duty and a lot should be said about that. When we consider people sitting on jury duty, it is a right and a privilege. Those people who are denied that right and privilege are not being dealt with fairly. When we say that you are going to sit on jury duty but you are not going to be able to collect unemployment insurance benefits, we are taking away their right.
I would like to put emphasis on other volunteers in a community. In my riding of Timmins-Chapleau we rely a lot on volunteers. We have numerous volunteer fire departments. We have a first response team in a town called Foleyet. A lot of people on that team are unemployed. A lot of our volunteer firefighters are unemployed.
The bill also asks for an exemption to the rule or a change in the rule for those people who provide food, flood control and shelter. We have an organization called the Lord's Kitchen which offers some 350 to 400 meals per week to underprivileged people, people who need help.
Are we telling all these volunteers who may in some cases be on unemployment insurance: "You can't do this on a continuous basis because you are not actively looking for work. You can't go out and help your community any more. You have to go out and look for a job"? Albeit they are looking for a job, does that mean that every waking moment they have to be out there banging on doors looking for work? Does that mean we have to deprive them of the opportunity of serving their community on a volunteer basis?
If that were the case, what would happen to the Cancer Society, the Heart Fund and the United Way, all those volunteer agencies that without volunteers will not exist? Is this the message that we are sending to our communities?
When we hear the government say "some of these areas fall within provincial jurisdiction", the government is passing the buck. The government is shedding itself of its responsibilities.
The government is not contributing to the UI fund. It is paid for by employers and employees. Why is there a problem with saying that people engaged in performing a civic duty or volunteer work cannot collect UI? Does that mean that those volunteers and those people who are performing jury duty are not actively seeking work?
They send out resumes. They fill out applications. They make appointments.
An employer will call you and say: "Come on in and let's have an interview." Does that mean that it has to be specifically at the time they are sitting on a jury, or could they make a time that is more convenient. Accommodations can be made. Potential employers, no. They are reasonable people and they know that when people are performing their civic duty, allowances have to be made.
I think this bill, as I said in the beginning, is a good bill. It is a clean-up bill. It is not one that is going to cost the government one red cent. If we look at the percentage of people who would be affected, the cost to the fund is very, very minimal but the benefit to the community is extremely large by having these people in place to perform these voluntary duties.
I do not really understand why the government members would want to rise in this House and speak opposing this bill. I would hope, as my friend from Restigouche- Chaleur has already pointed out, that this debate will take place in a non-partisan way, that when you look at the bill you look at the value of the wording, exactly what it will do. Never mind going outside the parameters and playing one political party against the other. I have no problem supporting this bill. It is a Liberal bill but it makes no difference. I would hope that the Conservative members will rise and speak their own minds as to exactly how they really feel about this bill. I am sure that in the end they will see that there is benefit, there is no cost, and that they, like us, will support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to the hon. member's bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
On the face of it, the hon. member's desire to amend this bill seems quite reasonable. Helping the community through volunteer work is a noble endeavour that benefits our society as a whole. However, Mr. Speaker, even if it may be the right thing to do, and I refer to making up for the financial losses of citizens when they take part in activities to help their community, we should ask ourselves how this should be done and

whether an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act is the right answer.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that although the amendment proposed by the hon. member is well inten-tioned, it is clear it is not up to the federal government to offer these people compensation through the Unemployment Insurance Act. Now, did you get that?
Consider the situation. From the outset, in the forties, the main objective of the Unemployment Insurance Act has always been to help workers "temporarily out of work". Canadians can be proud of this legislation because it is an integral part of programs that reflect our social responsibility. However, to make it effective, we have included measures to counter abuse and set criteria to ensure that the money paid during a period of unemployment goes to people who are out of work and are actively seeking a job. I emphasize, these people must be actively seeking employment. I am sure the hon. member will agree that without this provision, human nature being what it is, there would be considerable abuse of unemployment insurance funds. Section 14 of the Act, the section the hon. member wishes to amend, puts a heavy responsability on unemployment insurance recipients. I wish to quote subsection 14(a):
(a) capable of and available for work and unable to obtain suitable
employment on that day-
Mr. Speaker, under the Unemployment Insurance Act, the main concern of a person who is unemployed must be to seek employment, not for three or four days a week but every day. That person must look for a job and be immediately capable of accepting a suitable job offer.
Private Members' Business
I think the hon. member will agree it is reasonable to assume that if a person serves on a jury or works as a volunteer fireman, laudable though those activities may be, that person is not immediately available for work.
However, Mr. Speaker, the federal government realizes that sometimes there are special circumstances. That is why every application is assessed on its own merits, and as a result, decisions will vary. However, when a UI benefit recipient is selected as a jury member or as a member of a rescue team, if he makes arrangements to be called immediately as soon as suitable employment is available, and if that he then reports for work within 48 hours, then he is eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, I think the real problem is not the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act but the low rates of compensation paid by the provinces for jury duty. For instance, in Ontario, jury members receive nothing during the first ten days of a trial; from the eleventh to the forty-ninth day, they get only $40 a day, and starting on the fiftieth day, they receive $100 for their expenses. That is the rule in Ontario. Mr. Speaker, I have yet to see a single federal member urge the Government of Ontario to increase those amounts. They should, but I think they are asleep on the job.
Mr. Speaker, in Quebec they get $25 a day for the first ten days and $40 a day for subsequent days. In Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, employers are responsible for compensating employees who are called for jury duty. Unemployed workers in Newfoundland who are called for jury duty receive $4.75 an hour, but in Nova Scotia they only get $15 a day.
Mr. Speaker, I don't want to waste the precious time of hon. members by quoting figures for all the provinces. The ones I gave are fairly representative for the provinces as a whole. I hope opposition members understood those figures, and they should, if they can add and subtract. Suffice it to say that in general, the compensation paid by the provinces to persons serving on a jury is far less than UI benefits. However, I am sure hon. members will agree that UI benefits should not be used to subsidize provincial judicial systems.

October 8, 1991
Private Members' Business
UI benefit recipients who ask to be exempted from jury duty do so because the compensation is inadequate. Mr. Speaker, I think that judges who believe compensation paid by the provinces to persons who do jury duty is inadequate should do something about this problem. Mr. Speaker, despite the good intentions of the hon. member who proposed the amendment, the answer is not to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act but to ask the provinces to increase amounts paid to individuals who perform their civic duty by serving on a jury or working as volunteers in their communities.
I have reached the end of my speech, and I thank you, Mr. Speaker. I hope the Liberal member who tried to intervene during my speech listened to what I had to say.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
